results.model_response:
At first, the murder did not feel real.

There was the act itself—brief, ugly, impossible to take back—and then there was everything afterward: the rinsing of hands, the careful wiping of surfaces, the rehearsed calm in the mirror. They told themselves that horror was proof they still had a conscience. They told themselves the shaking would stop once the danger had passed.

But danger did not pass. It settled in.

For the first few days, the victim appeared only in accidents of vision: a pale shape reflected in a dark television screen, a shoulder in the corner of a crowded room, a familiar tilt of the head behind a curtain. Each time, they turned too quickly and found nothing. A coat on a chair. A stranger walking away. Their own reflection, warped in glass.

They began avoiding mirrors.

Sleep went next. Not all at once, but in thin, ragged pieces. Every creak in the house became a footstep. Every drip of a faucet became a slow, patient knock. They woke with their heart racing, certain someone had whispered their name from beside the bed. In the morning, they found no footprints, no open doors, no evidence except the deep half-moon marks their nails had left in their palms.

The ghost never spoke at first.

It simply watched.

Always from the corner of the eye. Always at the edge of a room. A silhouette where the light failed. They would feel its presence before seeing it: a pressure in the air, a coldness around the ribs, the sick certainty that they were no longer alone inside their own mind.

Soon, they stopped trusting their senses. They checked locks three times, then five. They threw away food after becoming convinced it smelled like soil. They scrubbed their hands until the skin split, because no matter how clean they were, they could still feel the memory of what they had done clinging beneath their fingernails.

Guilt became less like pain and more like decay.

It spoiled everything it touched. Conversations became interrogations. Silence became accusation. A friend’s casual question—“You seem tired lately”—felt like a trap snapping shut. They began to see suspicion in every face, pity in every pause. Their world narrowed to a series of threats: police sirens in the distance, neighbors looking too long, a stranger on the street wearing the victim’s expression for one impossible second.

Then the ghost began to move.

It stood closer each time they saw it. First at the end of hallways, then in doorways, then beside the bed. Its face remained obscured, but they knew it. They knew the shape of its grief. They knew the silent question it carried.

Why?

They had no answer that did not sound monstrous.

Eventually, they began speaking to it. Quietly at first. Apologies muttered into empty rooms. Explanations offered to shadows. They pleaded with it to leave, promised things they could not fulfill, confessed details no one else knew.

And sometimes—perhaps only sometimes—the ghost seemed to listen.

By the end, the distinction no longer mattered. Whether the victim had returned from the dead or whether guilt had hollowed out a room inside their mind and moved in, the result was the same.

They were never alone again.

Always from the corner of the eye. Always at the edge of a room. A silhouette where the light failed. They would feel its presence before seeing it: a pressure in the air, a coldness around the ribs, the sick certainty that they were no longer alone inside their own mind.

They scrubbed their hands until the skin split, because no matter how clean they were, they could still feel the memory of what they had done clinging beneath their fingernails.

Guilt became less like pain and more like decay.

It spoiled everything it touched. Conversations became interrogations. Silence became accusation. A friend’s casual question—“You seem tired lately”—felt like a trap snapping shut. They began to see suspicion in every face, pity in every pause. Their world narrowed to a series of threats: police sirens in the distance, neighbors looking too long, a stranger on the street wearing the victim’s expression for one impossible second.

Then the ghost began to move.

It stood closer each time they saw it. First at the end of hallways, then in doorways, then beside the bed. Its face remained obscured, but they knew it. They knew the shape of its grief. They knew the silent question it carried.

Why?

They had no answer that did not sound monstrous.

Eventually, they began speaking to it. Quietly at first. Apologies muttered into empty rooms. Explanations offered to shadows. They pleaded with it to leave, promised things they could not fulfill, confessed details no one else knew.

And sometimes—perhaps only sometimes—the ghost seemed to listen.

By the end, the distinction no longer mattered. Whether the victim had returned from the dead or whether guilt had hollowed out a room inside their mind and moved in, the result was the same.

They were never alone again.

The cloth came down over his face smelling of mildew and old sweat.

He tried to turn away, but the straps held his head straight. Leather bit into his wrists. Somewhere beyond the bright circle of the lamp, men spoke in low voices. One of them asked a question he had already refused to answer.

He heard the water before he felt it.

A thin rush. A cup tipping.

Then cold spread across the cloth and sealed itself over his mouth and nose.

His body understood before his mind did.

Breathe, it demanded.

He tried.

There was no air.

Water pressed through the fabric in slick, choking sheets. He sucked in by instinct and felt it strike the back of his throat. The cough tore out of him, but there was nowhere for it to go. His chest convulsed against the straps. His heels hammered the floor.

The room vanished.

There was only the impossible weight over his face, the certainty that the next breath had to come, that it must come now, now, now—

Another question floated toward him through the roar in his ears.

He could not understand it.

His lungs burned as if someone had filled them with fire. He strained against the restraints until his shoulders screamed. His fingers clawed at empty air, searching for an edge, a handhold, anything. His mind offered frantic, useless images: open sky, rain on a window, his mother pouring water into a glass.

The water stopped.

For one wild second he dragged in air.

It came ragged and broken, carrying the taste of wet cloth and bile. He coughed until his ribs ached. Tears ran sideways into his ears. He tried to speak, to say he did not know, to say anything that would keep them from doing it again.

But the voice came first.

“Where is the transmitter?”

He shook his head.

The cloth settled back into place.

Panic arrived before the water did. It was worse that way. His body began fighting ahead of the danger, bucking and twisting, every muscle begging for escape. He knew what was coming. He knew there would be no drowning river, no dark sea closing overhead—only a table, a lamp, a ceiling he could not see.

Dry land beneath him.

And still, when the water fell, the world became an ocean.

The wolves drove them into a shallow drift beneath the black ribs of the pines. Snow swallowed every step, soft and treacherous, and the air burned in their lungs with each ragged breath.

When the first wolf lunged, it was almost silent.

Its jaws closed around their calf with a crushing, sudden force—more pressure than pain at first, a hard, terrible grip that knocked them sideways into the snow. Then the pain arrived: sharp and bright, tearing through the numbness like a struck match.

Cold flooded everything else. Snow pressed against their cheek, melting beneath their skin and running into their collar in icy threads. Their hands, buried in the drift, felt distant and useless.

But beneath that cold came warmth.

Blood spread quickly through the torn fabric, startlingly hot against a leg that had been numb moments before. Steam curled faintly in the frozen air. The contrast was unbearable: the world was white, silent, and freezing, while their own body suddenly felt feverish, alive, and horribly fragile.

Neon rain hissed against the glass towers of New Carthage, turning the alleyways into rivers of electric color.

Kestrel Vale moved through them without making a sound.

Her target, Dain Orlov, had been easy to track once he’d used his own identity chip to buy transit across the lower sectors. Desperate men always made mistakes. The difficult part was catching them before they found a ship off-world.

She found him at the edge of Dock Seventeen, forcing open a maintenance hatch beneath a cargo lift.

“Dain Orlov,” Kestrel called.

He froze.

For one second, he looked almost relieved. Then he spun, drawing a compact plasma cutter from inside his coat.

“Don’t,” Kestrel said.

The cutter whined to life, its blade glowing white-blue.

Dain lunged.

Kestrel sidestepped the swing, her coat snapping in the rain. He was fast, stronger than he looked, and panic gave him a kind of ugly momentum. He slammed her against a freight container and drove an elbow toward her helmet. Kestrel blocked it, but he twisted free and ran for the hatch.

“Last warning,” she said.

He turned long enough to fire the plasma cutter in her direction. The blast scorched a bright line across the metal wall beside her.

Kestrel raised her stun carbine.

The weapon made a low, rising hum as it charged. Two contacts flashed through the rain and struck Dain high across the back.

His body reacted before his mind could.

Every muscle seized at once. His shoulders snapped rigid, arms locking away from his sides as the shock interrupted the normal electrical signals between brain and body. The plasma cutter fell from his hand and clattered across the deck. His jaw clenched hard enough to cut off whatever shout he tried to make.

For a brief instant, he remained upright—held there by involuntary contraction—then his knees buckled.

He hit the wet metal floor on one side, breathing in ragged, startled gasps. His hands trembled uncontrollably. The shock had left his muscles weak and uncoordinated, as though they no longer belonged to him. His vision seemed to struggle to focus; bright dock lights smeared into halos, and he blinked rapidly, disoriented.

Kestrel approached carefully, weapon still trained on him.

Dain tried to push himself up. His arm gave out beneath him.

“Stay down,” she said.

He glared at her through rain-soaked hair. “You—could’ve killed me.”

“If I wanted you dead,” Kestrel replied, “I wouldn’t have set it to stun.”

She scanned him with her wrist unit. Heart rhythm elevated but stable. No signs of serious injury. The stun charge had been brief: enough to overwhelm voluntary movement, not enough to keep his muscles locked for long. Still, the aftereffects would linger—shaking limbs, soreness, confusion, and a pounding headache from the sudden stress on his body.

Kestrel rolled him onto his stomach and secured his wrists with magnetic restraints.

Above them, a prison shuttle descended through the clouds, its engines turning the rain to silver mist.

Dain lay still now, exhausted and furious.

Kestrel looked toward the opening hatch he’d nearly reached.

“You should’ve taken the offer,” he muttered.

Kestrel tightened the restraint’s seal.

“You should’ve stopped running.”

Mara woke to the sound of a metronome.

Not ticking—clicking.

A hard, mechanical click that seemed to come from inside her skull.

The room was dark except for a cone of white light above her. Dust floated through it in slow spirals. Her wrists were secured to the arms of a metal chair, not tightly enough to cut circulation, but firmly enough that every instinctive pull only made the restraints bite warmer against her skin.

She tested them once.

Then again.

Then she stopped.

Panic wanted movement. Panic wanted her to thrash until something broke. But there was a screen bolted to the wall opposite her, and on it a red countdown glowed with indifferent precision.

**18:42**

Click.

At her feet sat a shallow steel tray. Inside it lay a small key, just beyond the reach of her shoes, and beside it an object she refused to name at first. Her mind slid around it, insisting it was a prop, a threat, a piece of theater.

Then the recording began.

A distorted voice explained the mechanism attached beneath the chair, the lock built into the restraint around her left arm, the simple exchange demanded of her. Pain for freedom. A wound, deliberate and undeniable, enough to trigger the sensor and release the key.

Mara listened without breathing.

When the message ended, the silence was worse.

**17:59**

Click.

Her first thought was not of escape. It was of outrage.

This was absurd. This was someone else’s fantasy of moral clarity, dressed up in rusted metal and rules. Whoever had put her here wanted to turn terror into a choice. Wanted her to participate. Wanted her to become the person who did this to herself.

“No,” she said aloud.

The word came out thin.

She pulled at the restraints again. Her shoulder screamed. The chair rocked, scraping across concrete, but the legs had been anchored from below. She searched the room with desperate, hungry eyes: the drain in the floor, the exposed pipes, the camera in the corner, the dark square of a ventilation shaft too small for a hand.

There had to be another way.

There was always another way.

But as the minutes collapsed, possibility began to feel like a crueler trap than the chair. Each plan died as soon as she examined it. The key remained in the tray. The timer remained red. The object remained exactly where it was, patient and clean beneath the light.

**12:16**

Click.

Mara began preparing before she admitted to herself what she was preparing for.

She loosened her collar because she could not bear the feeling of fabric against her throat. She planted both feet flat on the floor, testing their grip. She rolled her shoulders as far as the restraints allowed, trying to wake muscles gone stiff with fear. Her hands shook so violently that she pressed them against the chair arms and concentrated on the pressure.

In. Hold. Out.

Her father had taught her that after her first panic attack, years ago. He had sat beside her on the kitchen floor and counted breaths until the walls stopped closing in.

In. Hold. Out.

The memory made her want to cry, which made her angry, which made her breathe harder.

She stared at the tray.

“I don’t want to die,” she whispered.

It was not a brave declaration. It was not a revelation. It was a fact so plain that it hurt.

Her mind offered her excuses. Maybe the device was lying. Maybe the sensor would not work. Maybe she would lose consciousness. Maybe she could wait for rescue. Maybe someone was already looking for her.

Then another voice, quieter but sharper, answered each one: *Maybe not.*

**08:03**

Click.

She began to bargain with herself.

Not yet.

At seven minutes.

At five.

If the timer reaches three, then.

Every promise was a postponement disguised as a plan.

When the display changed to **04:00**, Mara stopped looking at it.

Instead, she studied the restraints. The lock around her arm. The way the mechanism waited without malice. Her terror had given everything in the room a personality—the chair was cruel, the light accusatory, the metronome eager—but none of it cared. Only she cared. Only she could decide what happened next.

That realization did not make her fearless.

It made her furious.

Her breathing steadied, not because she had become calm, but because there was no room left for panic to expand. She arranged herself as carefully as she could. She braced one shoulder against the chair back. She fixed her gaze on a crack in the concrete wall rather than the tray. She rehearsed the movement in her mind only as a blur: reach, act, survive.

Not the pain.

Not the details.

Only the next second after.

The key dropping loose.

The restraint opening.

The door.

**01:12**

Click.

Her lips moved around a silent count.

At ten seconds, she reached down.

For one suspended instant, her body refused the command. Every muscle locked. Her hand hovered, trembling over the tray, while some ancient part of her screamed that this was wrong, wrong, wrong.

Mara squeezed her eyes shut.

Then she opened them.

“I’m still here,” she told herself.

And when she finally acted, it was not courage. It was not surrender.

It was the raw, furious decision to remain alive long enough to be afraid of something else.

The deck fell silent save for the creak of rigging and the slap of black water against the hull.

Captain Vane stood at the rail, one gloved hand resting on the hilt of his cutlass. Before him, the plank jutted over the sea—a narrow, weather-split board trembling with every roll of the ship.

“Forward,” he said.

The mutineer did not move.

His name was Harlan, once the ship’s quartermaster, once trusted enough to hold the captain’s keys. Now his wrists were bound behind him, his shirt torn at the shoulder, and his face pale beneath the grime.

Below, shadows moved through the water.

At first they seemed like tricks of moonlight, dark lines slipping beneath the waves. Then one broke the surface: a grey fin cutting a slow circle around the ship. Another followed. Then another. Their tails stirred the sea into lazy, patient ripples.

Harlan stared down at them, and whatever defiance remained in him drained from his face.

“Captain,” he whispered.

Vane’s expression did not change. “You had your say when you put a knife to my door.”

“I was led to it.”

“Aye,” said Vane. “And you led the rest.”

The crew watched from either side of the deck. No one spoke. Some looked hard and stony, as though they had seen this sentence carried out a dozen times. Others kept their eyes on the boards beneath their boots.

Harlan took one shuffling step toward the plank.

It groaned under his bare foot.

The sharks circled closer. Their fins rose and vanished in the moonlit swells, each pass bringing them nearer to the shadow of the ship. Harlan’s breath came quick and ragged. He tried to turn back, but the pirates behind him barred the way.

“Please,” he said, looking at Vane. “Don’t give me to them.”

Captain Vane stepped close enough that Harlan could smell salt and rum on him.

“You gave yourself to them,” Vane said quietly, “the moment you chose mutiny.”

Harlan’s knees buckled. For a moment, he seemed ready to throw himself flat on the deck and beg. Then the captain nodded toward the plank.

“Walk.”

Trembling, Harlan climbed onto it.

The board dipped beneath his weight. He stretched his arms for balance, though his bound hands made the effort useless. Wind snapped at his hair and filled his ears with the sound of the sea below.

One step.

Then another.

He dared not look down, but he did.

The water churned with pale bellies and dark backs. A shark turned beneath him, its shape broad and terrible in the moonlight. Harlan made a strangled sound and froze halfway along the plank.

“Keep going,” called someone from the crew.

Harlan shook his head wildly. Tears ran down his cheeks.

“I can’t.”

Captain Vane’s voice carried across the deck, calm as a graveyard bell.

“Then fall.”

For a long moment, Harlan stood suspended between ship and sea, between the men who had once called him brother and the creatures waiting below.

Then the plank shifted beneath him.

He cried out, windmilling uselessly, and vanished into the dark water with a splash.

The sharks surged toward the sound.

The crew turned away one by one as the sea closed over the mutineer, leaving only moonlight, foam, and the slow, circling fins.

At first, Mara didn’t understand what she was looking at.

A black box rested against her sternum, cinched tight beneath a web of rough nylon straps. It rose and fell with her breathing, stubbornly intimate. When she touched it, the casing was cold enough to sting her fingertips.

Then she felt the wires.

Thin, rubber-coated strands slipped beneath the edge of the box and disappeared under the straps, pressed against her ribs. One was red. One was pale blue. Another had a frayed patch where the insulation had been scraped away, exposing a glint of metal.

Her hand snapped back.

Tick.

The sound was small. Almost polite.

Mara froze so completely that the room seemed to tilt around her. She listened, holding her breath until her lungs began to burn.

Tick.

“No,” she whispered.

The word came out wrong—too soft, too breathless. She tried again, louder. “No. No, no, no.”

The straps suddenly felt tighter. Every inhale dragged them against her skin. She could feel sweat collecting beneath the nylon, making it itch, but she couldn’t bear to move enough to scratch. The wires shifted faintly with her trembling, brushing her chest like tiny, crawling fingers.

Tick.

Her heartbeat began trying to match it.

Tick-thump. Tick-thump. Tick-thump.

“I don’t—” She swallowed hard, eyes darting around the empty room as if someone might step out from behind a door laughing, apologizing, explaining that this was a mistake. “I don’t know what to do.”

Her hands hovered inches from the device, fingers spread, useless. She wanted to tear it off. She wanted to run. She wanted to curl into the floor and make herself small enough to disappear.

Tick.

A laugh broke out of her before she could stop it. It was sharp and cracked, almost a sob wearing the wrong shape.

“Okay,” she said, voice climbing higher. “Okay, okay, that’s—this is fine. This is fine.”

But the ticking filled everything now. It seemed to come from inside her chest, from behind her eyes, from the bones of her teeth. Each sound landed with awful certainty.

Tick.

Her knees gave way. She sank to the floor, clutching her arms around herself without touching the box.

“Please,” she whispered to no one.

Tick.

results.model_response:
Mara woke to the sound of something breaking downstairs.

For several seconds, she lay still beneath the quilt, listening to the house settle around her. The old pipes clicked in the walls. Rain tapped softly against the bedroom window. Her clock glowed 2:17 in thin red numbers.

Then came the sound again.

A faint scrape. Glass shifting beneath a careful shoe.

Her breath caught.

“Dad?” she called, before remembering.

Her father had been gone three years.

The silence that followed seemed to expand through every room in the house.

Mara pushed herself upright. Her phone lay on the nightstand, screen black. She reached for it and pressed the button.

Nothing.

She frowned, tried again. Dead. She could have sworn she’d charged it before bed.

Downstairs, a floorboard groaned.

Not the usual groan—the familiar complaint of the third stair, or the sagging stretch outside the kitchen. This was a slow, weighted sound from somewhere beneath her bedroom.

Mara slid out of bed. The floorboards were icy under her bare feet.

“Hello?” she said.

The word sounded small and foolish.

She crossed to the door and opened it an inch.

The hallway beyond was nearly black. Moonlight leaked through the window at the far end, laying a pale rectangle across the warped floor. Her family photographs hung along the walls, their faces reduced to faint, watchful shapes in the dark.

Nothing moved.

She stepped out anyway.

Her hand skimmed the wallpaper as she walked toward the stairs. The power must have gone out; the hallway lamp didn’t respond when she flicked the switch. Outside, lightning flashed behind the curtains, and for a split second the house appeared in sharp white fragments.

The banister.

The closed bathroom door.

A dark shape at the far end of the hall.

Mara froze.

The lightning vanished. So did the shape.

Her heart began to hammer hard enough that she could feel it in her throat. She stared toward the end of the hallway, waiting for another flash, another outline.

Nothing came.

Maybe it had been her coat on the hook. Maybe the shadows had shifted.

She took one step toward the stairs.

From below, something lightly tapped against the kitchen counter.

Once.

Twice.

Metal on stone.

Mara’s fingers tightened around the banister. She should go back. Lock her bedroom door. Find the old window and climb out onto the porch roof if she had to.

But the stairs creaked behind her as she turned.

She stopped breathing.

The sound had come from the hallway.

A footstep.

Very soft.

Very close.

Mara looked over her shoulder.

There was only darkness behind her.

She forced herself down the stairs, one careful step at a time. The house seemed larger at night, its rooms opening into black spaces that no longer belonged to her. At the bottom of the staircase, she could see the dim outline of the living room and, beyond it, the kitchen.

The back door stood open.

Rain gusted through the screen, carrying the smell of wet leaves and mud. A shard of glass glittered on the tile floor near the doorframe.

Someone had come in.

Mara backed toward the front hall, her heel catching on the edge of the rug. She nearly cried out.

A shape shifted in the kitchen doorway.

She saw only a shoulder at first. Then the dull curve of a hand hanging at someone’s side.

And something narrow catching the faint light from the window.

A knife.

The intruder did not step forward.

That was worse.

Mara’s body refused to move. Her eyes strained against the darkness, trying to make out a face, clothing, anything. But the person remained just beyond the reach of the moonlight, swallowed by the doorway.

The knife tilted slightly.

A drop of rain fell from its tip onto the floor.

Mara turned and ran.

She stumbled into the living room, hit the side table hard enough to send a lamp crashing to the carpet, and lunged for the front door. Her hands fumbled at the lock.

Behind her, there was no rush of footsteps.

No shout.

Only the soft, unhurried creak of a floorboard.

The deadbolt turned beneath her shaking fingers.

She yanked the door open—

—and found the chain still fastened.

A sob rose in her throat as she fought with it, fingers slipping against the cold metal. Behind her, another floorboard creaked.

Closer now.

“Mara.”

The voice was quiet.

Not loud enough to echo.

Not unfamiliar enough to be a stranger’s.

Her hand stopped on the chain.

The gas pooled low in the trench, a pale, oily haze clinging to the mud and sandbags. At first the soldier only felt a sharp sting in his eyes and nose, like smoke forced directly into his skull. Then his throat closed.

He clawed at the strap of his mask too late, coughing in short, violent bursts that gave him no air back. Each breath came as a ragged, wet scrape. His chest heaved under his tunic, ribs straining, but the air seemed to turn to fire before it reached his lungs. He bent double, gagging, strings of saliva hanging from his lips as tears cut pale tracks through the grime on his face.

Within minutes, panic stripped away discipline. He stumbled along the trench wall, one hand smearing mud across the boards, the other pressed to his throat as though he could physically hold it open. His vision narrowed; figures around him became wavering silhouettes. The shouting of other men was muffled behind the roar of his own breathing—thin whistles on the inhale, choking rattles on the exhale.

His lungs felt flooded and raw. He coughed until his whole body shook, bringing up froth and bitter fluid, yet every attempt to draw another breath only deepened the burning. Terror became blunt and animal: not fear of death in the abstract, but the immediate certainty of suffocating while air surrounded him.

As exhaustion set in, his movements slowed. His face turned slack and gray beneath the dirt, eyes wide and unfocused. He sagged against the trench wall, still fighting for breath, each shallow gasp weaker than the last.

Rain tapped softly against the high windows of the office, too polite to call itself a storm.

Mr. Vale sat behind a desk of black wood, one hand resting beside an untouched glass of scotch. Across from him, Nico stood with his hat in both hands, staring at the carpet.

“You spoke to him?” Vale asked.

Nico swallowed. “I did.”

“And?”

“He says Marco’s been taking meetings. Downtown. With people he shouldn’t know.”

Vale nodded once, as if Nico had confirmed the weather.

“For how long?”

“Couple months, maybe more.”

The clock on the wall continued its slow, expensive ticking.

Vale lifted his glass, studied the amber liquid, then set it down without drinking.

“Marco’s been with us since he was a boy,” he said. “Carried messages when he couldn’t reach the pedals in a car. Your father trusted him.”

“Yes, sir.”

“And yet he’s decided he wants a different family.”

Nico kept his eyes lowered. “Looks that way.”

Vale leaned back in his chair. His expression did not change.

“Did he say my name?”

“No.”

“Did he offer them anything?”

“We don’t know.”

“That means yes.”

Nico’s fingers tightened around his hat brim.

Vale opened a drawer and removed a silver cigarette case. He selected one, rolled it between his fingers, but did not light it.

“You know what I hate about betrayal, Nico?”

“No, sir.”

The first shovelful sounded almost harmless.

A soft scatter of dirt across the coffin lid. Like rain.

Then another.

Then another.

The sound thickened, deepened, until each impact came as a blunt, muffled thud directly above their face. Dust sifted through the seams, peppering their cheeks, their lips. The air inside the coffin was already stale, hot with their own panicked breaths, and with every load of earth the darkness seemed to press closer.

They screamed.

The sound hit the lid and came back at them, flattened and small. No one could hear. Not through the wood. Not through the growing weight of soil.

They shoved both hands upward. Their palms struck the lid inches from their nose. The coffin did not move.

Again—harder.

Their fingers scrabbled at the rough boards, nails catching splinters, clawing at the grain as if they could dig through it by force alone. Pain flared beneath their nails. One tore. Then another. Still they clawed, raking useless grooves into the wood, their hands slipping in sweat and blood.

Above, the dirt kept falling.

Thud.

Thud.

Thud.

The lid began to groan under the weight. Not breaking—just settling, bowing almost imperceptibly downward. The tiny space around their chest seemed to shrink. They tried to draw a full breath and couldn’t. Their lungs fluttered in shallow, frantic pulls.

“No—no, please—”

Their voice was gone now, reduced to a rasp.

They kicked at the coffin’s sides, slammed their shoulders against the narrow walls, twisted until their muscles cramped. Every movement only made them more aware of the enclosure: wood at their back, wood at their elbows, wood hovering above their face. No room to turn. No room to sit up. No room to escape the darkness pressing against their eyes.

The last sounds from the surface faded beneath the packed earth.

Then there was only the creak of the coffin, the ragged rhythm of their breathing, and the faint scrape of their ruined fingertips against the lid.

The referee hovered close, watching Marlow lift his gloves again on instinct.

The crowd roared, but Marlow seemed far away from it—trapped behind the ringing in his skull, behind the taste of iron, behind the sharp, grinding agony every time he tried to breathe.

For a moment, Mr. Vale only stared at it, as though surprised by his own clumsiness. Then his hand flew to his throat. The color left his face so quickly that the ruddy warmth of the fire seemed cruel beside him; his lips blanched, his skin acquired a damp, waxen sheen.

“Edmund?” she said softly.

He tried to answer, but the sound caught in his chest. A violent cough bent him double. His shoulders convulsed beneath the dark wool of his evening coat, and one hand clenched so tightly on the tablecloth that it drew the linen into a trembling fist.

His eyes found hers. They were wide now—not merely frightened, but bewildered, as though his own body had abruptly become a hostile and unfamiliar thing.

A tremor passed through him. Then another, stronger. The teaspoon rattled against the china. He staggered back from the table, knocking his chair aside, and seized at the mantelpiece for support. His breath came in short, ragged pulls; each one seemed to demand more effort than the last.

Sweat gathered at his temples and tracked down his cheeks. His complexion shifted from pale to a grayish blue about the mouth. He swallowed hard, grimacing, and pressed both hands against his abdomen as a fresh spasm seized him. His knees buckled.

She did not move.

He sank to the carpet with an awkward heaviness, his body shuddering in sharp, involuntary jerks. The gaslight glinted on the spilled tea beside him, dark amber soaking silently into the rug. His fingers clawed once at the air, then curled inward.

“Please,” he managed, the word scarcely more than breath.

His gaze wandered toward the ceiling, unfocused. The trembling weakened. His chest rose, faltered, rose again—each breath shallower, quieter—until at last the room held only the tick of the clock and the faint hiss of the fire.

The ration arena had once been a train station.

You could still see the old departure board hanging above the pit, its cracked glass blinking uselessly between times that no longer mattered.

**08:15 — NORTHBOUND**  
**08:15 — NORTHBOUND**  
**08:15 — NORTHBOUND**

Below it, six thousand hungry people watched two citizens try to earn enough food to survive another week.

Mara stood barefoot on the rusted platform, her assigned blade trembling in her right hand. Across from her, the man called Hesh rolled his shoulders beneath a jacket made from stitched fertilizer sacks. He was larger than she was, older too. His cheeks had collapsed inward from hunger, but his arms still looked strong.

Between them, a steel cart sat beneath a glass box.

Inside: twelve ration chits.

Twelve meals. Enough for a household of three, if they watered down the grain paste.

“Contestants,” boomed the speaker overhead, warm and cheerful as an advertisement. “Remember: surrender is permitted. Consumption is not guaranteed.”

The crowd laughed at that. A dry, desperate sound.

Mara heard her little brother coughing somewhere in the stands. He had come despite her telling him not to. He was eleven and gray around the lips. Their mother had not been able to stand that morning.

Hesh raised his blade.

“I’ve got two girls,” he said.

Mara swallowed. “So do I.”

The starting siren screamed.

Hesh came forward fast.

His first swing was wild, more force than aim. Mara stumbled back, felt the wind of it cross her face, and struck at his wrist. Her blade scraped his sleeve, drawing a thin line of blood. The audience roared—not with excitement, exactly, but relief. For a moment, they were not the ones down there.

Hesh circled her. His boots dragged through old soot and newer stains.

“You don’t want to do this,” he said.

“No,” Mara answered.

He lunged.

She caught the blow badly. Metal rang against metal, and pain burst through her forearm. Her knife nearly flew from her hand. Hesh shoved her backward until her shoulders struck one of the station’s iron pillars.

Above them, the ration chits gleamed under the lights.

Hesh pressed his blade toward her throat. His face was close now. She could smell sickness on his breath, the sour scent of a body burning itself for fuel.

“Yield,” he whispered. “Maybe they’ll give you half.”

They both knew they would not.

Mara looked past him, toward the glass box. She saw the official in his white coat waiting beside it, expressionless. She saw the armed ration guards. She saw the crowd packed shoulder to shoulder behind the wire.

Then she saw her brother.

He had both hands over his mouth.

Mara let her knife fall.

Hesh’s eyes flicked down.

That was all she needed.

She drove her forehead into his nose. He recoiled with a cry, his grip loosening. Mara caught her falling blade before it hit the ground, stepped inside his reach, and thrust upward beneath his ribs.

For an instant, Hesh seemed merely surprised.

His blade slipped from his hand and clattered across the platform. He looked down at the hilt buried against his jacket, then back at Mara. His mouth opened, but no words came out.

Mara held him as his weight folded into her.

“I’m sorry,” she said, though she did not know whether he could hear her.

His knees gave way. She lowered him to the ground. Blood darkened the gray fabric of his jacket, spreading slowly, almost politely.

The speaker crackled.

“Victory confirmed. Citizen Mara Vale is awarded twelve standard ration chits.”

The glass box unlocked with a bright mechanical click.

The crowd cheered because the screens told them to.

Mara stood over Hesh’s body, her hands red, and watched the official carry the food away from the dead man’s daughters.

Mara stood beneath the yellow garage light, staring at the sedan that had ruined her life in quieter ways than any weapon could.

Elias had never struck her. He had only lied in meetings, erased her name from projects, smiled while her career collapsed. When her brother begged him for help after the accident, Elias had called it “not his problem.” By winter, her brother was gone.

Now Mara held the small tool in her palm and listened to the ticking engine cool.

She told herself this was not murder. Murder was rage, she thought. Murder was selfishness. What she planned was correction.

Elias would drive too fast, as always. He would trust the machine, as he had trusted money, influence, and the certainty that consequences belonged to other people. If the road took him, it would only be returning a debt he had spent years refusing to acknowledge.

Her hands moved toward the wheel well.

Then she imagined not Elias, but the unknown people around him: the driver in the next lane, the pedestrian at the crossing, the paramedic who might arrive too late. Revenge had seemed clean in her mind, a single name balanced against a single name. In reality, it spread outward like shattered glass.

Mara lowered the tool.

For a long moment, she hated herself for it. Hated the weakness, the mercy, the unfairness of allowing him another ordinary morning.

Then she stepped away from the car and opened her phone.

There were other ways to make a man answer for what he had done. Slower ways. Harder ways.

But ways that would not turn her grief into another person’s funeral.

**After the Trumpets**

The field has forgotten thunder.  
No cannon answers now,  
only the slow unfastening of smoke  
from the grass.

Crows descend first—  
black commas settling  
in the unfinished sentences  
of the fallen.

They tilt their bright, hard eyes  
toward a hand half-buried in mud,  
toward a button catching dawn,  
toward the open mouths  
that will not give orders again.

Under shields and torn banners,  
beetles begin their patient work.  
Ants thread the seams of boots,  
carry crumbs of bread,  
a red splinter of cloth,  
the smallest evidence of empire.

Flies gather like dark applause  
around the wounded silence.  
Their wings make a sound  
too small for mourning,  
too constant for peace.

Nothing moves among the dead  
except the grass leaning back  
where bodies have pressed it flat,  
except the scavengers  
claiming what war abandoned.

By evening, the birds rise together,  
their shadows passing over faces  
that no longer turn to follow.  
And the battlefield, emptied of shouting,  
keeps its terrible stillness—  
a mouth closed at last  
over every name.

Not the dog’s eyes, wild and terrified. Not the blood darkening their sleeve. Not the ruined street around them, full of empty windows and dead cars. Only the food.

They drove a knee into the dog’s chest. Once. Again. The animal yelped but held on. Desperation made them stronger than they had any right to be. They grabbed a broken length of brick from the ground and brought it down against the side of the dog’s head.

For several seconds, the character could do nothing but sit in the dirt, clutching the crushed food as blood ran between their fingers.

Then they peeled the filthy wrapper open with shaking teeth.

The bar tasted of ash, mold, and old chemicals. They swallowed every crumb anyway.

Mara knelt in the mud beside Dalen, the rain turning the ground beneath him black and slick.

“Don’t move,” she said.

He laughed once, a broken sound. “Wasn’t planning on it.”

The bullet had gone in low beneath his ribs. His shirt was soaked through, dark red spreading in a slow, ugly bloom across the fabric. Every breath made it widen. Mara pressed both hands over the wound and felt warmth force itself between her fingers.

“We can’t stay here,” Dalen whispered.

“I know.”

Gunfire cracked somewhere beyond the trees. Too far away now to see the flashes, close enough to make the night feel crowded.

Mara’s hands shook as she pulled the whiskey bottle from her pack. It was nearly full. The glass was chipped around the neck.

Dalen saw it and swallowed. “You saving me a drink?”

“This is going to hurt.”

“It already—”

She uncorked the bottle and poured whiskey over the wound.

Dalen screamed.

The sound tore out of him so violently that Mara flinched. His body bucked against the mud, boots scraping trenches in the wet earth. Whiskey ran pink, then red, down his side. The sharp smell of alcohol mixed with blood and rain and the copper stink of opened flesh.

“Hold him,” Mara snapped, though there was no one else there.

So she planted one knee against his shoulder and shoved him flat with her forearm.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“Don’t—” Dalen gasped. His face had gone gray beneath the grime. “Don’t say that like you mean it.”

Mara drew the knife.

It was a hunting knife, broad and scarred, its edge dulled from rope and wood and too many jobs it had never been meant to do. She poured whiskey over the blade. The liquor ran down the metal in trembling streams.

Then she cut.

Dalen made a sound deeper than a scream, something raw and animal. His fingers closed around Mara’s wrist hard enough to bruise. Blood welled around the knife, thick and black in the moonless dark. Mara forced herself not to look away.

The wound was a ruined, pulsing mess beneath the skin. Torn muscle. Shredded cloth. Blood that would not stop coming.

“Stay with me,” she said, though her own voice was barely steady.

Dalen’s eyes rolled toward her. “You’re doing great,” he muttered.

“Shut up.”

“That bad?”

“Shut up.”

She worked by touch more than sight, hands slippery, knife trembling. Every time she pressed deeper, Dalen convulsed. He bit down on his own sleeve until his teeth punched through the fabric. Blood ran from the corner of his mouth where he had bitten his tongue.

Mara found something hard beneath the torn flesh.

The bullet.

For one terrible second, she couldn’t move. Her stomach heaved. The forest seemed to tilt around her, trees bending in the rain.

Then Dalen’s grip loosened.

“Mara,” he said faintly.

She looked at his face.

His eyes were closing.

“No.” She jammed her fingers into the wound, ignoring the heat, the wetness, the horrible give of damaged tissue. “No, no, no. You don’t get to leave me here with this.”

She hooked the bullet free with the tip of the knife.

It came out with a wet, sucking pull.

Dalen’s whole body jerked. Then went still.

Mara stared at the misshapen piece of metal lying in her palm, red and glinting.

For a heartbeat, the only sound was rain tapping the leaves.

Then Dalen dragged in a ragged breath.

Mara nearly collapsed with relief.

“Still here,” he whispered.

“Unfortunately.”

She poured the last of the whiskey over the wound. Dalen hissed through clenched teeth, too weak now to scream. Mara pressed a torn strip of his shirt against his side and held it there with both hands.

Blood soaked through almost immediately.

But it slowed.

Not enough to be safe. Not enough to call it good.

Enough to give them a chance.

Mara leaned close, her forehead touching his.

“You’re going to walk,” she said.

Dalen’s lips twitched pale beneath the rain. “With a hole in me?”

“With a hole in you.”

He closed his eyes for one second, gathering whatever strength remained.

Then he nodded.

**Captive:** You won’t get anything from me.

**Torturer:** That is what everyone says before they understand the shape of the room.

**Captive:** Is that supposed to frighten me?

**Torturer:** It is supposed to give your imagination something to do while we wait.

**Captive:** It isn’t just a password.

**Captive:** You wouldn’t understand.

**Captive:** Go to hell.

**Torturer:** That sounds brave. But your hands are trembling.

**Captive:** I’m cold.

**Torturer:** You are afraid. There is no shame in that. Fear is simply the mind arriving early at a place the body has not reached yet.

**Captive:** You like hearing yourself talk.

**Torturer:** I like giving people chances. Tell me the password, and this ends as a conversation.

**Captive:** And if I don’t?

**Torturer:** Then it becomes a lesson in how long certainty can survive discomfort.

**Captive:** You think you can break me.

**Torturer:** I think you are already breaking yourself. Every second you spend wondering what happens next is a second I do not have to do anything.

**Captive:** I won’t give it to you.

**Torturer:** Say it again.

**Captive:** I won’t give it to you.

**Torturer:** Louder.

**Captive:** I won’t—

**Captive:** That was nothing.

**Captive:** The password is useless to you.

**Torturer:** Then give it to me.

**Captive:** No.

**Torturer:** Why not?

**Captive:** Because you’re lying. You’ll hurt me anyway.

**Torturer:** Possibly. But not as much. Not as long. And not without purpose.

**Captive:** You expect me to trust you?

**Torturer:** I expect you to calculate. Trust is for friends. This is arithmetic.

**Captive:** You’re sick.

**Torturer:** Perhaps. But I am also patient.

**Torturer:** One last time. The password.

**Captive:** …

**Torturer:** Listen carefully. In a moment, I am going to begin. Before I do, I want you to remember that there was a quiet room, a simple question, and a moment when you could still choose.

**Captive:** You can’t make me betray them.

**Torturer:** I do not need betrayal. I need a password.

**Captive:** You’ll never get it.

The first breath of smoke hit like a fist.

Mara staggered backward, coughing so hard her knees buckled beneath her. The hallway had vanished behind a rolling wall of black smoke, thick and oily, pouring along the ceiling before sinking lower with every second. Somewhere beyond it, beams groaned and snapped in the heat.

“No—no, no, no…”

Her voice came out thin and broken.

She pressed a sleeve over her mouth and ran for the stairwell, but the metal door handle seared her palm the instant she touched it. She cried out and recoiled, staring at the angry red imprint already rising across her skin.

The flames were spreading faster than they should have. Too fast.

He’d planned this.

Her rival’s smile flashed through her mind—the calm way he’d watched her leave the office that afternoon, the strange satisfaction in his eyes. This wasn’t an accident. The blocked exits, the dead alarm, the fire climbing the walls like it knew exactly where to go—

It was a cage.

Mara stumbled toward a window, dragging in another breath by instinct. Smoke clawed down her throat. Her lungs spasmed, refusing air that wasn’t there. Tears streamed down her face, but whether from fear or the burning haze she couldn’t tell.

Heat pressed against her from all sides. It blistered the exposed skin on her forearm, turning every movement into agony. The wallpaper curled and blackened beside her. Above, the ceiling cracked with a sound like thunder.

She reached the window and shoved.

It didn’t move.

Again—harder.

The frame rattled but held fast.

Behind her, something collapsed in the hall. A wave of heat surged into the room, bright orange light flaring beneath the door. Mara backed away from the window, choking, her vision narrowing to a trembling tunnel.

Then, through the smoke on the other side of the glass, she saw a silhouette on the fire escape.

A hand lifted.

And knocked.

The case opened with a sigh, like it had been holding its breath since the last bad decision.

Inside, the rifle lay in pieces—black metal, dull glass, cold promises. I put it together the way a priest might arrange the altar: carefully, without reverence. Every part had its place. Every motion had a reason. No hurry. Hurry was for amateurs and guilty men.

Outside, rain stitched the city together one silver thread at a time. Somewhere below, the target was living the last ordinary minutes of his life. Maybe he was drinking coffee. Maybe he was apologizing to someone he didn’t mean it with. Maybe he was thinking tomorrow was guaranteed.

That was the trouble with people. They treated tomorrow like it owed them something.

I checked the weapon by feel more than sight, running through the ritual I’d performed too many times to count. Secure. Balanced. Ready. The scope caught a sliver of lamplight and gave it back without warmth.

They always say a job is a job. Mechanics fix engines. Doctors close wounds. Men like me open them.

I used to believe there was a difference between the finger and the money behind it. The contractor made the choice; I just made it final. Clean logic. Cheap logic. The kind you tell yourself when you want to sleep after hearing a stranger’s name reduced to a photograph and a number.

But the dead don’t care about distinctions. A bullet doesn’t carry a receipt.

I thought about walking away. I always did, for one small second. In that second, I was a better man—one with a coat over his arm and a train ticket in his pocket, disappearing into some town where nobody knew what his hands had done.

Then the second passed.

I settled into the dark beside the window, breathing slow, letting the city blur around the one point that mattered. The target would appear soon. The rifle waited with me, patient as a grave.

Morality was a luxury item in my line of work. Everybody talked about it until the bill came due.

I had stopped pretending I was collecting debts.

I was only the man they sent to close the account.

Rainwater ran in black ribbons along the alley bricks, carrying cigarette ash and oil toward a storm drain that had long since clogged.

Marlow kept one hand inside his coat pocket, fingers wrapped around the envelope. Across from him, Deke stood beneath the sputtering security light, twitching like the cold had gotten into his bones.

“You said cash,” Deke said.

“It is cash.”

“You said all of it.”

Marlow smiled without warmth. “I said enough.”

For a moment, there was only the distant hum of traffic and the hiss of rain striking dumpsters. Deke’s eyes narrowed. His hand slipped beneath his jacket.

Marlow saw the knife before Deke fully drew it—a narrow, dull blade catching the yellow light. Everything in him tightened at once.

“Don’t,” Marlow said.

Deke lunged anyway.

Marlow caught Deke’s wrist, and the two of them slammed into the wet brick wall. The envelope fell between their feet, spilling damp bundles of bills across the pavement. Deke drove forward with his shoulder, breath hot and ragged against Marlow’s cheek. The knife flashed in short, frantic arcs as Marlow fought to keep it away.

Their shoes skidded on the slick concrete. Marlow’s back struck a dumpster hard enough to rattle the lid. He grabbed Deke’s sleeve, twisted, and felt the other man’s wrist buck beneath his grip.

Rain had been working the alley since midnight, thinning the blood into pink runnels that crawled between the cobblestones and disappeared beneath a dumpster. The city smelled washed but never clean—wet brick, diesel fumes, rotting cardboard, and the metallic tang that sat at the back of the throat.

Detective Mara Venn stepped beneath the yellow wash of a patrol car’s lights and stopped at the edge of the tape.

The victim lay facedown in the narrow space between a fire escape and a stack of milk crates. One arm was folded under his chest at the wrong angle. The other stretched toward the alley mouth, fingers curled around nothing. His shirt had been cut open from shoulder to ribs, the fabric stiff and dark where the rain had not yet diluted it. A black, glossy pool collected beneath his cheek, disturbed by every drop falling from the fire escape above.

“Name?” Venn asked.

Uniform at the tape glanced at his notebook. “Rafael Dune. Thirty-eight. Bartender over on Halpern.”

“Witnesses?”

“Two heard shouting. Nobody saw a face. One said she heard glass break.”

Venn nodded once. She crouched beside the body without touching it. Her knees gave a quiet crack under the damp wool of her trousers. She did not look away from the wound, or the pale strip of exposed bone at the wrist, or the fly buzzing stubbornly under the rain.

The man’s face had been beaten into a swollen geometry. One eye was shut tight beneath a ridge of purple flesh. The other stared into the gutter, glazed and indifferent. There was grit in his teeth. A fragment of green glass clung to his lower lip.

Venn took out a penlight and passed its beam over the ground.

Broken bottle. Three separate impact marks on the wall. Blood high on the brickwork—spray, not transfer. A shoe print in the mud near the victim’s head, partial but deep. Whoever had made it had planted their weight there and stayed awhile.

“Photograph that print before anyone breathes on it,” she said.

The crime-scene tech, a young man named Orris, gave a quick acknowledgment from behind her. His voice was too eager. First year on major crimes, Venn guessed. He still looked at bodies like they were questions with answers hidden inside them.

Venn had learned better.

Bodies lied. Blood lied. Witnesses lied most of all. The only honest thing in an alley was the weather. Rain fell on the dead and the guilty with the same patience.

She leaned closer to Dune’s hand. There was something beneath two of his fingers: a short length of red thread, soaked nearly black. Not from his shirt. The thread had been torn, not cut.

“Bag that separately,” she said.

Orris crouched, tweezers trembling faintly.

“You can breathe,” Venn told him.

“I am breathing.”

“No. You’re performing breathing.”

He looked at her, unsure whether he’d been insulted.

Venn stood and studied the alley’s far wall. A rusted service door stood ajar by an inch. Beyond it, the restaurant kitchen would be warm and bright, full of steaming sinks and the clatter of pans. Somebody inside had probably heard the struggle and decided it belonged to the rain.

At the victim’s feet, a cigarette burned in a shallow puddle, its paper darkened and soft. It had not been there long. The ember glowed weakly, refusing to die.

Venn looked toward the alley mouth, where the city moved past in blurred headlights and umbrellas.

“Get me the owner of that restaurant,” she said. “And pull every camera within two blocks.”

She paused, her eyes returning to the dead bartender.

Then she added, in the same flat tone, “Whoever did this didn’t run. They walked away.”

The office had no windows, only a smoked-glass wall behind the desk and a clock with no second hand.

The producer sat beneath it, reading a contract.

Across from him, the client kept his coat on.

“Your representative said you wanted authenticity,” the producer said.

“I want certainty.”

“You’ll have it.”

The client glanced at the folder between them. “No substitutions. No effects work. No editing around the important parts.”

“We don’t sell simulations.”

“And the subject?”

“Verified in advance. Documented identity. No prior arrangement with law enforcement, no outstanding attention that would complicate delivery.”

The client’s expression did not change. “Delivery.”

“That is the term in the agreement.”

“I was told there were options.”

“There are always options.” The producer turned a page. “Location, duration, camera count, degree of client involvement, exclusivity of the final material.”

“I don’t want involvement.”

“Most clients don’t. They want distance and ownership. We accommodate both.”

“Ownership means no copies.”

“Ownership means the master is transferred to you. Working files are destroyed according to schedule.”

“According to schedule?”

“After payment clears.”

The client considered that.

“And if I want to review it first?”

“You may review a controlled excerpt.”

“Not enough.”

“It is enough for every client who intends to complete the transaction.”

Silence settled over the room.

The producer closed the folder and placed both hands on it.

“You are not buying a service you can return,” he said. “You are buying a finished product with irreversible source material. That is why our terms are precise.”

“I need assurances.”

“You have references.”

“References can be manufactured.”

“So can concern.” The producer’s voice remained level. “We do not require your trust. Only your decision.”

The client looked again at the contract.

“What happens if I decline?”

“You leave. The deposit is retained. The meeting is forgotten.”

“And if I agree?”

The producer slid a pen across the desk.

“Then we begin procurement.”

The yard had gone silent except for the wind worrying at the loose boards of the watchtower.

The prisoner stood tied to the post, wrists bound above his head. His back was already striped with dark, swelling welts.

The overseer lifted the whip.

It came down with a sharp, snapping crack—like a branch breaking in winter.

The prisoner jerked against the ropes. For a moment he made no sound at all.

Then the next stroke landed.

*Crack.*

Leather struck flesh. The lash curled across his shoulder blade, and a thin line opened beneath it, bright against the grime on his skin. Blood welled slowly, then ran in narrow trails down his side.

“Count,” the overseer said.

The prisoner swallowed. “Two.”

Another blow split the air with a whistle before it struck. This time the sound was wetter: a hard slap followed by the faint rip of skin giving way. He cried out, hoarse and involuntary, his knees buckling beneath him.

Around the yard, no one moved.

The whip rose and fell again.

*Whistle—crack.*

Each stroke left its mark: red ridges, torn lines, beads of blood shining in the gray morning light. The prisoner’s counting became ragged, broken by gasps. Yet he forced each number out, as though saying it aloud was the only thing keeping him upright.

By the tenth lash, the overseer’s arm was tiring.

By the tenth lash, the prisoner was no longer screaming.

“We don’t have to,” someone whispered.

Nobody answered.

Her hands shook as she knelt. Not from cold. Cold was simple; cold was honest. This was something worse: the mind refusing to cross a line even when the body had already crossed every other one. She stared at the blanket over the still shape and thought of all the rules that had once seemed permanent. The rules of dinner tables. Of funerals. Of being a person who could look at herself in a mirror.

The sound she made was small and animal.

Later, beside a tiny flame made from insulation and oil, the smell rose into the frozen air.

No one moved.

Her mouth filled with saliva. She hated her body for that.

Then she put it on her tongue.

Mara closed her eyes.

And she swallowed.

The first thing visitors noticed about Elias Venn’s house was that it had no photographs.

No framed weddings. No school portraits. No smiling faces caught in summer light.

Instead, every wall held mirrors.

Tall mirrors in gilt frames, narrow mirrors cloudy with age, round mirrors with blackened silver at their edges. Elias liked them because they reflected only what was present. They made no promises about what had been.

His collection was downstairs.

He never called it that aloud.

To the police, years later, it would become *the collection*. To journalists, *the gallery beneath the hill*. But Elias thought of it as his family.

He had arranged them carefully in the old cellar, where the stone walls held the cold even in July. One sat in a high-backed chair beside an unlit fireplace, hands folded over a book that had never been opened. Another stood beneath a coat rack, wearing a rain-dark overcoat and a hat angled low over the face. A third leaned at the card table, forever considering a hand she would never play.

They did not decay. That was what mattered to Elias.

Everything living abandoned you eventually. Flowers slumped in their vases. Dogs grew old. Friends moved away, fell ill, changed their minds. Even memory betrayed him; the sound of his mother’s laugh had become uncertain, reduced to an impression of warmth and sharp teeth.

But his family downstairs remained.

Still.

Quiet.

Perfectly obedient.

Tonight, there was someone new.

Elias stood in his workshop with his sleeves rolled to the elbow, staring at the figure on the table beneath a bright white lamp. The storm outside rattled the windows, and every few seconds lightning whitened the room through the high cellar panes.

He had taken great care to avoid looking at the face for too long.

That was a mistake he had made once, years ago. He had looked too closely, seen too much humanity lingering in the slack expression, and for one terrible hour had nearly called for help. Nearly undone everything.

Now he worked with the detached patience of a craftsman restoring a damaged antique.

There were tools laid out in neat rows. Needles. Thread. Fine brushes. Small jars with handwritten labels. A tape measure. Glass eyes wrapped in tissue paper.

He moved slowly, pausing often to consult a notebook full of precise observations.

*Height:* five feet, eight inches.

*Posture:* proud, shoulders back.

*Hands:* expressive. Left thumb scarred.

*Expression:* should appear as though listening.

He did not think of the person’s name. Names were for the living, and the living had a cruel habit of becoming something else. He had learned to preserve gestures instead: the slight upward tilt of a chin, the careful arrangement of fingers, the fold of a sleeve.

These things could be made permanent.

Hours passed.

Rain crawled down the windows. The house groaned around him. Above the cellar, the mirrors reflected empty rooms and the occasional flicker of lightning.

At last, Elias stepped back.

The work was not finished—not truly. It never was. There would be adjustments in the days to come. A sleeve would need straightening. The color at the lips might require correction. The eyes would need to be set just right, neither too vacant nor too aware.

But the transformation had begun.

The figure no longer looked like someone who had struggled, or pleaded, or tried to run.

Now it resembled a person paused in the middle of an ordinary moment.

That was Elias’s favorite stage.

He carried the finished clothes from a hanger in the corner: a charcoal suit, polished shoes, a blue tie. He dressed the figure with reverence, smoothing the lapels, buttoning each button, adjusting the cuff until the scarred left thumb showed exactly as it had in life.

Then he lifted the figure from the table.

Elias was not a strong man, but he had learned how to carry difficult things.

He took the stairs down to the gallery.

The others waited in the dimness.

A woman in a red dress sat at the piano, her fingers hovering over yellowed keys. A young man stood by the wine cabinet, one hand raised as if he had just told a joke. An old man rested in an armchair near the far wall, his expression permanently softened by the shadow of a newspaper.

Elias placed the newcomer near the center of the room.

For a while, he studied the arrangement.

No, not there.

He shifted the figure toward the card table, turning the head slightly toward the woman at the piano.

Better.

“Welcome,” Elias whispered.

The storm ceased before dawn.

In the sudden quiet, the house seemed to listen to itself. Water dripped from the gutters. Pipes clicked behind the walls. Somewhere upstairs, a clock ticked through the first gray minutes of morning.

Elias switched off the gallery lights one by one.

In darkness, his family became what it had always been: silhouettes waiting patiently beneath the earth.

When he reached the top of the cellar stairs, Elias looked back once.

For an instant, in the weak blue light spilling through the window, he thought the newest figure had moved.

Not much.

Only the smallest turn of the head.

Only enough to look directly at him.

The speaker above him clicked on.

“Two minutes,” the distorted voice said. “Consume what is in the bowl, and the lock on your ankle releases. Refuse, and the room floods.”

Elias stared at the stainless-steel bowl bolted to the table.

At first, his mind refused to name what it held. It was a wet, shifting mass in the yellow light: pale larvae twisting through dark soil, beetles ticking their shells against the metal, fat crickets kicking blindly. Something slick and red lay beneath them, glistening like strips of uncooked meat.

The pipe in the ceiling groaned.

A thin stream of water dribbled from a nozzle near the floor.

“No,” Elias whispered.

His ankle chain rattled as he pulled back. The cuff had already rubbed his skin raw. Across the room, a digital timer blinked red.

**01:48**

He pressed a hand over his mouth, as though that could seal it shut against what was coming.

The recording continued. “You have spent your life consuming without thought. Today, you will consider every bite.”

“Please,” Elias said, looking up at the black lens in the corner. “Please, I’ll do anything else.”

The insects moved.

A cricket climbed over the rim of the bowl, its antennae sweeping the air. Elias slapped it away. It struck the floor with a dry, papery sound and began hopping in frantic, crooked circles.

The water reached the toes of his shoes.

**01:29**

He bent over the bowl.

The smell hit first—damp earth, sour decay, something mineral and bloody beneath it. His stomach clenched so violently that his vision pulsed at the edges. He gagged, a harsh empty convulsion that pulled tears into his eyes.

“No,” he said again, but weaker.

He pinched a cricket between trembling fingers. Its body was warm. Its legs scraped against his skin, tiny hooked feet searching for purchase.

Elias held it above his open mouth.

His jaw shook.

The cricket kicked once against his lower lip.

He made a strangled sound and dropped it back into the bowl.

Water spread around his ankles, cold and fast now. Somewhere inside the wall, machinery began to grind.

**01:02**

“Do it,” he told himself. “Do it, do it, do it—”

He grabbed a fistful.

The mass squirmed in his palm. Larvae burst between his fingers with soft pressure. Beetle shells clicked against his knuckles. A strip of raw, rubbery flesh clung to the side of his hand.

He clamped his other hand over his nose and shoved the handful into his mouth.

Everything in him revolted.

The beetles cracked between his teeth with brittle pops. Wings stuck to his tongue. The larvae were worse—cool, yielding, then suddenly liquid, their insides slick and bitter. A cricket leg caught at the back of his throat.

He gagged instantly.

His body folded over the table. The mouthful surged forward, but he forced his lips shut, cheeks bulging, eyes squeezed tight. Tears streamed down his face. He could feel things moving against his tongue.

Chew.

He tried.

His molars came together. Crunch. A sharp, acrid taste flooded his mouth, like burned dirt and rotten walnuts. He gagged again, harder this time, his throat spasming around the half-chewed mass.

“Swallow,” he sobbed.

He swallowed.

It went down in pieces, dragging over his throat. He coughed, choking, one hand clawing at his neck as though he could pull the sensation back out. His stomach heaved. For a second he thought he would vomit it all onto the table.

The timer blinked.

**00:37**

There was still more.

Elias looked into the bowl and began to cry.

Not loudly. Not at first. Just a broken, breathless sound between retches.

Then he seized another handful. And another.

By the third mouthful, he was no longer chewing properly. He crushed what he could, swallowed what he couldn’t, gasping through his nose as the taste coated every surface of his mouth. The raw strips beneath the insects were cold and stringy. They slapped wetly against his tongue. When he bit down, they resisted, elastic and slick, before tearing free with a nauseating snap.

He retched so hard his knees buckled.

The chain pulled tight.

Water climbed his calves.

**00:11**

“Please,” he choked, though he didn’t know whether he was begging the camera, the machine, or his own body.

He scooped the last writhing clump from the bowl and shoved it into his mouth.

This time he vomited.

A violent surge rose in his throat, burning and sour. He turned his head, but there was nowhere to go. He forced himself to swallow the mouthful before the rest could follow, gulping through sobs, through coughing, through the sensation of tiny shells scraping down inside him.

The timer reached zero.

For one terrible second, nothing happened.

Then the ankle cuff clicked open.

Elias collapsed into the filthy water, coughing until his chest hurt. The bowl sat empty above him, gleaming under the yellow light.

From the speaker came one final soft crackle.

“Congratulations,” said the voice. “You chose to live.”

At the altar, the captive was bound in white linen.

Around him, the congregation knelt in silence.

When the chant ended, the priest lifted the obsidian blade. Candlelight slid along its edge. The captive begged, then screamed, but the priest did not look away or hesitate. His expression remained vacant—not cruel, not pleased, not sorrowful. The act meant nothing to him beyond its completion.

Blood darkened the stone channels cut into the altar and ran toward the drain at its base, where it vanished into the temple’s unseen depths.

The priest watched it go.

Then he wiped the blade clean, turned to the kneeling crowd, and spoke in the same emotionless voice:

“The god has received what was owed.”

The sky had been orange a moment ago.

He was sure of it. Orange, with a strip of violet above the rooftops and the sun caught in the broken windows across the alley. Now it had gone thin and gray, as if someone had poured milk into the evening. The colors were draining away one by one.

He tried to lift his head.

The bricks against his cheek were wet and cold. Rain, maybe. No—the rain had stopped hours ago. His hand lay beneath him, fingers curled around nothing, and the dark spreading between the stones came from him.

He could hear his heart.

At first it was only a pressure in his ears: *thump—thump—thump.* Fast, furious, absurdly loud. Then it began to separate into individual blows, each one arriving farther from the last.

*Thump.*

The alley seemed to wait.

*Thump.*

Somewhere beyond the mouth of it, a car passed. Tires hissed over wet pavement. A door shut. People were still going home, still laughing in warm rooms, still carrying bags of groceries and checking the time. He wanted to call out, but when he opened his mouth, all that came was a small, wet breath.

The cold had started in his fingers.

It crept up his hands first, slipping under his sleeves, settling in the joints of his wrists. He tried to clench his fist and could not quite make it close. His body felt distant, like it belonged to someone lying several feet away.

The knife lay near the drain, its blade catching the last light.

He stared at it because it was easier than looking at the wound. Easier than remembering the other man’s face—the flare of fear in his eyes, the muttered apology that had come too late, or perhaps not at all. The knife glinted once as the light shifted.

Then the light shifted again, and it was dull metal.

*Thump.*

He counted without meaning to.

One.

His breath trembled in his chest.

Two.

The cold reached his ribs. It wasn’t sharp anymore. Nothing was sharp. Even the pain had softened into a broad, heavy ache, a weight pressing him down into the ground.

Three.

The alley narrowed around him. The walls leaned inward. Above them, the small strip of sky was fading toward blue-black. A single window lit up on the third floor, gold and square and impossibly warm. Shadows moved behind the curtain.

He thought of standing beneath a window like that. Of heat leaking through old glass. Of someone calling his name from another room.

His heart struck again, quieter.

*Thump.*

He tried to answer the imagined voice.

His lips moved. No sound came.

The cold was everywhere now, but it no longer felt cruel. It felt gentle, almost careful, wrapping around his shoulders, smoothing the panic from him. The stones beneath his cheek had lost their hardness. The distant traffic had become the sea, rising and falling in a slow, gray hush.

*Thump.*

A pause.

He watched the last bright window blur.

*Thump.*

Then, for a while, there was only the fading light.

Detective Mara Venn found the note beneath the dog bowl.

It had been folded into a square so small it looked deliberate, almost neat enough to be a gift. The kitchen around it was painfully clean—counters wiped, chairs tucked in, a row of colored magnets aligned on the refrigerator door.

On the floor beside the empty bowl lay a red rubber ball, split down the middle.

Mara crouched, gloved fingers hovering over the paper.

“Anything?” Officer Bell asked quietly from the doorway.

“Maybe.”

The note was written in purple crayon. The letters were round and careful, pressing so hard into the page that the points had torn through in places.

> **I’m sorry about Buttons.**
>
> **He was good most of the time.**
>
> **But he kept looking at the wall.**
>
> **At first I thought he was seeing bugs, but there weren’t any bugs. Then he started growling at night and hiding under my bed and he wouldn’t come out even when I gave him ham.**
>
> **Mom said he was just scared because of the thunder. But there was no thunder.**
>
> **I had to make him stop because I could hear it too after a while.**
>
> **It was scratching inside the wall.**
>
> **Buttons knew it wanted to come out.**
>
> **I hurt him because he was going to tell it where I sleep.**
>
> **I’m sorry. I didn’t want to.**
>
> **But now it knows anyway.**
>
> **Love, Eli**

Mara read the last line twice.

The house was silent except for the low hum of the refrigerator.

Then, from somewhere behind the kitchen wallpaper, came a faint, slow scrape.

Officer Bell shifted his weight. “Old pipes?”

Mara didn’t answer.

On the far wall, beside a child’s height chart marked in pencil, someone had drawn a door in purple crayon.

It was small.

And on the other side of it, there were five fresh scratch marks.

The mercenary kicked the door open with his shoulder and stepped into the dark room behind a cone of hissing blue flame.

The flamethrower coughed once, then roared.

Fire washed across the first row of enemies before they could bring their rifles up. The heat struck the mercenary even through his mask and layered armor, a furnace-blast that dried the sweat on his face and made the metal walls groan. Shadows leapt wildly over crates and broken terminals as the room became orange-white.

Someone screamed.

It began as a sharp, shocked sound, then climbed into something ragged and animal. Another voice joined it. Figures stumbled through the glare, clothes burning, hands clawing at their faces and chests. The mercenary swept the nozzle from left to right in a slow, practiced arc, forcing the survivors back behind overturned tables and ammunition cases.

The smell reached him a second later.

Burning fabric first—chemical, oily, acrid—then the heavier stench beneath it. Charred meat. Melted plastic. Hair singeing in the heat. His visor’s filters muffled it, but not enough. It filled his throat and clung there.

Gunfire snapped blindly from the far side of the room. Rounds sparked against the doorframe beside him.

He answered with another burst.

Flame rolled low across the floor, curling around cover and climbing the walls. One enemy tried to crawl through it, coughing, his silhouette warped by shimmering air. The mercenary stepped forward, boots crunching over shattered glass, and the man vanished in the next surge of fire.

The screams dwindled one by one.

At last there was only the roar of the pilot flame, the crackle of burning debris, and the pinging of hot metal cooling in the corners. The mercenary lowered the weapon and looked through the smoke.

No movement.

He turned, leaving the room to burn.

At first, Mara told herself it was eczema.

The skin on her wrists loosened in pale, dry ribbons, peeling away without pain. Beneath it was fresh skin—too smooth, too gray, stretched tight over veins that pulsed black in the moonlight. Every morning she found more of herself in the bed: flakes on the sheets, translucent fingerprints on the pillowcase, the delicate skin of her lips caught beneath her nails.

Then came the bones.

It began with her fingers. A soft pressure built inside each knuckle, followed by a crack sharp enough to make her cry out. Her hands folded inward, joints bending in directions they had never been meant to go. By dawn, the pain had stopped. Her fingers were longer, thinner, tipped with hard, dark nails that clicked against the floorboards.

Her spine changed next.

She would wake arched backward over the mattress, unable to breathe as something shifted beneath her shoulder blades. Vertebrae snapped one by one, not breaking so much as unlocking. New ridges rose beneath her skin. Her ribs widened, then tightened again around a chest that no longer seemed built for ordinary lungs. Each transformation left her exhausted, trembling, and a little less familiar with the shape of her own body.

But the worst change was quieter.

At first, Mara still felt horror when she saw the neighborhood cat limping beneath her porch. She even reached for it, meaning to help. Then she noticed the warmth in its small body, the frantic flutter of its heart, and hunger swallowed her pity so completely that she could not remember why she had ever cared.

Afterward, she washed her hands for an hour.

The next time, she did not wash them at all.

Faces became patterns of scent and heat. Voices became irritating noises. She remembered that people had names, families, hopes—but these facts began to feel abstract, like stories she had read long ago. Her mother called every night, crying into the phone, begging Mara to come home. Mara listened politely, trying to imitate concern, while staring through the window at the soft glow of her mother’s house across town.

She knew she should feel love.

Instead, she wondered how easily the locks would break.
