The first shovelful sounded almost harmless.

A soft patter against the coffin lid. Loose earth scattering over wood.

Elias lay still beneath it, wrists burning against the rope, cheek pressed to the velvet lining. For one absurd second, he thought of rain. Rain on a roof. Rain on the old tin shed behind his childhood home.

Then the second shovelful landed.

Thud.

The whole box trembled.

Dust sifted down through the seams, settling on his lips. He coughed, and the sound came back to him immediately—small, muffled, swallowed by the narrow walls inches from his face.

“No,” he whispered.

There was no room to turn his head fully. His knees were bent awkwardly beneath the lid, shoulders pinned by the coffin’s narrow sides. When he tried to lift his chest for a deeper breath, the lid hovered close above him, close enough that his knuckles struck it when he raised his hands.

Another shovelful.

Thud. Scrape.

The sound was heavier now. Not rain anymore. Not even footsteps.

It was the sound of a world being placed on top of him.

“Stop!” Elias shouted.

His voice struck the lid and died. He shouted again, harder, tearing at his throat.

“STOP! I’M HERE!”

Above him, something shifted. For half a heartbeat, hope flared—someone had heard, someone was coming back—

Then the dirt fell again.

Thud.

A weight pressed down over his chest, not physically, not yet, but in his mind. He imagined the grave filling. Dirt pouring over the lid, packing around the sides, climbing past the handles, swallowing the last thin spaces where air might have moved.

He sucked in a breath.

The air smelled wrong: damp wood, old fabric, soil. Every breath warmed it further. Every exhale seemed to linger in the coffin, hovering around his face, waiting to be breathed in again.

He kicked at the foot of the box.

The impact jolted pain through his heels. The coffin barely moved.

“Please,” he said, though no one could hear him.

The dirt came faster.

Thud.

Thud.

Thud-thud-thud.

Each impact sent a dull vibration through the lid and into his bones. Fine soil spilled through a crack near his temple. He twisted away from it, but there was nowhere to go. It crawled into his hair, along his neck, beneath his collar.

His breathing became quick, shallow. He tried to slow it. Tried to count.

One breath in.

One breath out.

But the air was already thick. His lungs worked harder for less. He opened his mouth wide, dragging in what he could, and tasted earth.

The lid creaked.

Elias froze.

Above him, the dirt shifted with a deep, settling groan. The coffin seemed to tighten around him. Not actually moving, perhaps—but he felt it shrinking, felt the dark pressing inward against his eyes, his ribs, his thoughts.

He slammed both palms against the lid.

Once.

Twice.

Again.

The blows became weaker almost immediately. The wood answered with a hollow, buried sound, as though he were knocking from the bottom of a lake.

“Help,” he gasped.

The word barely existed.

The final shovelfuls were different. Duller. The earth above had grown deep enough to cushion the impacts. Instead of sharp thuds, there came a dense, distant pressure—heavy soil settling into place.

Then silence.

Not true silence. There was his breathing: ragged, wet, too loud in the cramped dark. His heartbeat hammered in his ears. Somewhere above, dirt slid against dirt with a faint granular whisper.

But the voices were gone.

The footsteps were gone.

Elias lay in the blackness, eyes open, staring at a lid he could not see.

He drew in another breath.

And another.

Each one smaller than the last.

They called it the Improvement Ward.

The name was painted in soft blue letters above the steel doors, cheerful as a nursery sign. Beneath it, the line moved forward in silence.

Mara stood between a woman who had once been a teacher and a boy who could not have been older than sixteen. Their wrists were bound in clean white bands. Each band bore a barcode, a district number, and the word *VOLUNTARY*.

No one had volunteered.

Beyond the doors came a steady mechanical rhythm: drills, pumps, the faint metallic click of tools being set down. Every few minutes, another person emerged from the far end of the ward.

They walked upright. That was the first thing Mara noticed.

They walked with perfect posture and identical strides, their faces pale beneath fresh bandages. A thin black seam ran from behind each ear down the side of the neck, disappearing beneath gray work uniforms. Their eyes did not settle on anything. They stared forward, pupils reflecting the overhead lights like polished lenses.

“Asset thirty-two,” a nurse called.

The teacher beside Mara flinched.

“Asset thirty-two, advance.”

“I have a name,” she whispered.

The nurse did not look up from her clipboard. Two guards took the woman by the arms and led her through the blue doors. Her shoes squeaked once on the tile, then the sound was swallowed.

Mara tried to remember the teacher’s name. She had heard it in the line, spoken quickly before the guards approached.

Elena, perhaps.

Or Elira.

Already it was fading.

When Mara’s turn came, they placed her on a narrow table beneath a circle of white light. Straps closed over her ankles, her chest, her forehead. The material was warm, almost gentle. That frightened her more than cold metal would have.

A surgeon leaned over her. His face was hidden behind a clear shield.

“Citizen,” he said, “you have been selected for service adaptation.”

“I work in the archives,” Mara said. Her voice shook. “I’m not sick.”

“This is not treatment.”

He held up a small metal device, no larger than a finger. It pulsed faintly in his gloved hand.

“Then what is it?”

“A correction.”

The first incision was only pressure, a distant dragging sensation at the base of her skull. Then something opened inside her—a bright, blinding pain that did not seem to belong to flesh. Her body arched against the straps. She screamed until her throat tore raw, but the room did not change. The surgeons continued speaking calmly over her.

“Neural relay stable.”

“Motor interface responding.”

“Suppress emotional volatility.”

At that, Mara fought harder.

She thought of her apartment: the crooked kitchen window, the chipped yellow cup she used every morning, the dust-heavy smell of old paper in the archives. She seized those memories as if they were handles above deep water.

Her mother’s laugh.

Rain against glass.

The name of the teacher in the line.

Elena. It was Elena.

But each memory became harder to hold. The device beneath her skull sent cold signals through her thoughts, smoothing away panic, then grief, then anger. The pain remained, but it began to feel distant, like a report being read about someone else.

A voice spoke inside her head.

**STAND.**

Her legs moved.

Mara wept, though she no longer understood why. Tears ran into her ears as the straps released. She sat upright with precise, borrowed motion. Her hands lifted before her face.

They were still her hands.

But they trembled only when commanded.

A technician adjusted a dial near her collarbone. Something clicked beneath her skin. The pain vanished.

So did the urge to scream.

“Designation assigned,” the surgeon said. “Asset thirty-three. Labor division.”

Mara tried to say her name. She knew that she had one. It was important. There had been someone who called her by it. There had been a life arranged around its sound.

Her mouth opened.

“Asset thirty-three,” she said.

The surgeon nodded with quiet satisfaction.

Outside, the city’s factories burned red beneath a black sky. Thousands of altered workers crossed the streets in ordered lines, carrying steel, clearing rubble, assembling machines that would one day replace the hands assembling them.

Mara joined them.

Somewhere behind the commands, behind the measured steps and regulated breath, a small part of her still remembered a yellow cup and rain on a window.

It knocked once against the walls of her mind.

Then the system instructed her to keep walking.

By the time Mara Vale arrived, the rain had stopped.

It hung in silver beads from the iron fence around the old conservatory, each droplet catching the patrol lights and breaking them into small, trembling stars. The building had once belonged to a botanical society, the kind that believed a greenhouse could improve the moral character of a city. Now its glass panes were cracked, its white-painted frame furred with rust, and ivy had found its way through every weakness.

“Victim’s inside,” Detective Harlan said.

Mara nodded without looking at him.

She was already studying the entrance.

A muddy footprint on the threshold. A bent brass latch. A line of damp leaves arranged—not scattered—along the floor just beyond the doorway. Their stems all pointed inward.

Someone had thought about direction.

“Don’t touch anything,” Harlan said.

“I know.”

But she did not move for several seconds. She stood beneath the broken archway and let the scene reveal its first impression.

Most people saw violence as an interruption. A rupture. A terrible mess imposed on an ordinary room.

Mara had learned that it could also be composed.

That realization had come years earlier, at her first major case: a body recovered from a burned apartment, posed by accident beneath a fallen chandelier. Its crystals had spread across the floor in a glittering radius. Every shard had reflected the blackened walls. Everyone else had seen destruction.

Mara had seen symmetry.

She had hated herself for it.

Then, slowly, she had stopped hating herself. She told herself that noticing was not admiring. That beauty and goodness were not twins. That a trained eye had to recognize pattern wherever it appeared—in blood spatter, in footprints, in the deliberate placement of a chair.

But lately, the distinction had begun to blur.

Inside the conservatory, the air smelled of wet soil, stagnant water, and old roses.

The victim lay at the center of the tiled floor.

Mara’s first thought was that he had been placed beneath the ruined dome to receive the sky.

The cloud cover above had thinned, and pale morning light filtered through the fractured glass. It fell in long geometric panels across his suit: gray, blue, white, gray again. Around him, hundreds of dead camellia blossoms had been arranged in widening circles, their petals bruised dark at the edges. The flowers were not fresh. They had been gathered from somewhere else, carried here, and placed one by one.

The man’s name, Harlan told her, was Arthur Bell. Fifty-seven. Antiques dealer. No sign of forced struggle beyond the entrance. No weapon visible.

Mara barely heard him.

Bell’s hands had been folded over his chest. Between them rested a small brass key.

His face had been turned toward the roof, eyes closed, expression almost peaceful.

That was what made it obscene.

The murderer had understood something about the human eye: how it sought resolution, how it relaxed when disorder became pattern. The circles of flowers drew the gaze inward. The broken panes above formed an imperfect halo. Even the water dripping from the roof struck the tiles at measured intervals, like a metronome.

Mara crouched at the edge of the nearest ring.

“Don’t step inside,” she said to the crime-scene photographer.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were thinking about it.”

The photographer gave her a wary look.

Mara swallowed. “Sorry.”

She adjusted her gloves and examined the petals. Some were flattened on one side. Others had a dusting of pale grit.

“Cemetery soil,” she said.

Harlan raised an eyebrow. “You can tell that from flowers?”

“Maybe. The soil is too chalky for this place.”

She leaned closer. There was a faint scent beneath the rot—something medicinal, sharp and green. Not perfume. Crushed stems.

Her mind began assembling the scene in layers.

The victim had known the killer, or had been convinced to enter willingly. The leaves at the door had been placed after the fact, perhaps to conceal tracks, perhaps as an invitation. Bell had been washed. His suit had been changed; the fabric at his cuffs was dry despite the rain. The key in his hands belonged to an old-fashioned cabinet lock, not the conservatory.

And the flowers—

The flowers had been selected for their color after decay.

Not red, not white. Brown at the edges. Cream at the center. Beautiful only in the moment before becoming refuse.

Mara felt a cold admiration stir in her chest.

It was not for the death. Never for that.

It was for the patience.

The killer had spent hours creating this. They had carried flowers through rain. They had arranged each circle by hand. They had chosen a neglected glass house because dawn would do the rest.

A person had died, and someone had made that death into an argument.

Mara rose too quickly. The room tilted.

“You okay?” Harlan asked.

“Yes.”

He watched her, unconvinced. “You’ve got that look.”

“What look?”

“The one you get when you’re solving it before the rest of us have caught up.”

Mara looked again at Arthur Bell beneath the shattered ceiling.

“No,” she said quietly. “This isn’t solving.”

The photographer’s camera clicked. The sound was abrupt, practical, almost comforting.

Mara walked toward the far wall, where old planting tables stood beneath a sheet of cracked glass. On one table rested a single blue vase. It had been cleaned recently; rainwater had not yet dulled its surface.

Inside was one living camellia.

White.

Its stem had been cut cleanly.

Mara stared at it for a long time.

Then she saw the tiny streak of soil on the vase’s rim, and beneath it, a partial fingerprint in damp clay.

Evidence.

Not art.

Evidence.

The thought steadied her, though not completely.

Later, in the laboratory, she would identify the soil, trace the vase to a funeral home, match the key to a locked drawer in Bell’s shop. She would find records of a woman whose family heirlooms Bell had sold fraudulently, a woman who had spent years tending graves in the city cemetery and studying the old conservatory’s decay.

There would be an arrest. There would be interviews, reports, a courtroom, photographs projected on clean white walls.

The scene would become evidence, then paperwork, then memory.

But for years afterward, Mara would dream of the conservatory at dawn.

Not of the victim’s face.

Not of the killer.

Of the dead flowers arranged in perfect circles, turning slowly darker as the rainwater gathered at their edges.

And in the dream, she would stand at the doorway, unable to enter, unable to leave, terrified by the part of herself that still wanted to know who had made something so terrible look almost sacred.

Then, slowly, she had stopped hating herself. She told herself that noticing was not admiring. That beauty and goodness were not twins. That a trained eye had to recognize pattern wherever it appeared—in blood spatter, in footprints, in the deliberate placement of a chair.

But lately, the distinction had begun to blur.

Inside the conservatory, the air smelled of wet soil, stagnant water, and old roses.

The victim lay at the center of the tiled floor.

Mara’s first thought was that he had been placed beneath the ruined dome to receive the sky.

The cloud cover above had thinned, and pale morning light filtered through the fractured glass. It fell in long geometric panels across his suit: gray, blue, white, gray again. Around him, hundreds of dead camellia blossoms had been arranged in widening circles, their petals bruised dark at the edges. The flowers were not fresh. They had been gathered from somewhere else, carried here, and placed one by one.

The man’s name, Harlan told her, was Arthur Bell. Fifty-seven. Antiques dealer. No sign of forced struggle beyond the entrance. No weapon visible.

Mara barely heard him.

Bell’s hands had been folded over his chest. Between them rested a small brass key.

His face had been turned toward the roof, eyes closed, expression almost peaceful.

That was what made it obscene.

The murderer had understood something about the human eye: how it sought resolution, how it relaxed when disorder became pattern. The circles of flowers drew the gaze inward. The broken panes above formed an imperfect halo. Even the water dripping from the roof struck the tiles at measured intervals, like a metronome.

Mara crouched at the edge of the nearest ring.

“Don’t step inside,” she said to the crime-scene photographer.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were thinking about it.”

The photographer gave her a wary look.

Mara swallowed. “Sorry.”

She adjusted her gloves and examined the petals. Some were flattened on one side. Others had a dusting of pale grit.

“Cemetery soil,” she said.

Harlan raised an eyebrow. “You can tell that from flowers?”

“Maybe. The soil is too chalky for this place.”

She leaned closer. There was a faint scent beneath the rot—something medicinal, sharp and green. Not perfume. Crushed stems.

Her mind began assembling the scene in layers.

The victim had known the killer, or had been convinced to enter willingly. The leaves at the door had been placed after the fact, perhaps to conceal tracks, perhaps as an invitation. Bell had been washed. His suit had been changed; the fabric at his cuffs was dry despite the rain. The key in his hands belonged to an old-fashioned cabinet lock, not the conservatory.

And the flowers—

The flowers had been selected for their color after decay.

Not red, not white. Brown at the edges. Cream at the center. Beautiful only in the moment before becoming refuse.

Mara felt a cold admiration stir in her chest.

It was not for the death. Never for that.

It was for the patience.

The killer had spent hours creating this. They had carried flowers through rain. They had arranged each circle by hand. They had chosen a neglected glass house because dawn would do the rest.

A person had died, and someone had made that death into an argument.

Mara rose too quickly. The room tilted.

“You okay?” Harlan asked.

“Yes.”

He watched her, unconvinced. “You’ve got that look.”

“What look?”

“The one you get when you’re solving it before the rest of us have caught up.”

Mara looked again at Arthur Bell beneath the shattered ceiling.

“No,” she said quietly. “This isn’t solving.”

The photographer’s camera clicked. The sound was abrupt, practical, almost comforting.

Mara walked toward the far wall, where old planting tables stood beneath a sheet of cracked glass. On one table rested a single blue vase. It had been cleaned recently; rainwater had not yet dulled its surface.

Inside was one living camellia.

White.

Its stem had been cut cleanly.

Mara stared at it for a long time.

Then she saw the tiny streak of soil on the vase’s rim, and beneath it, a partial fingerprint in damp clay.

Evidence.

Not art.

Evidence.

The thought steadied her, though not completely.

Later, in the laboratory, she would identify the soil, trace the vase to a funeral home, match the key to a locked drawer in Bell’s shop. She would find records of a woman whose family heirlooms Bell had sold fraudulently, a woman who had spent years tending graves in the city cemetery and studying the old conservatory’s decay.

There would be an arrest. There would be interviews, reports, a courtroom, photographs projected on clean white walls.

The scene would become evidence, then paperwork, then memory.

But for years afterward, Mara would dream of the conservatory at dawn.

Not of the victim’s face.

Not of the killer.

Of the dead flowers arranged in perfect circles, turning slowly darker as the rainwater gathered at their edges.

And in the dream, she would stand at the doorway, unable to enter, unable to leave, terrified by the part of herself that still wanted to know who had made something so terrible look almost sacred.

The cottonwood stood alone at the edge of town, its branches black against the red evening sky.

Nobody spoke while they worked the rope over the lowest limb. The sheriff’s hands were steady, though his jaw clenched hard enough to show white beneath the stubble.

“You got anything to say?” he asked.

The condemned man stood on the back of a wagon, wrists bound behind him. Dust clung to his boots and blood had dried dark along one side of his face. He looked over the gathered townsfolk—the widows, the ranch hands, the men with their hats crushed in both fists.

“No,” he said.

The sheriff gave a small nod.

The wagon driver snapped the reins.

The horses lurched forward.

For an instant, the man seemed to hang in the air, balanced between breath and death. Then the rope went taut.

A sharp, dry crack cut through the silence.

Several people flinched. One woman covered her mouth. The man’s body jerked hard at the end of the rope, boots kicking at nothing. His heels beat once against the empty air, then again, weaker. His fingers curled and uncurled behind his back. The rope creaked above him as his weight swung slowly beneath the branch.

Dust settled in the wagon tracks.

After a few long moments, the twitching became a faint shudder running through his legs. Then even that faded. He turned gently in the evening wind, a dark shape beneath the cottonwood, while the town stood watching and no one found a word worth saying.

The alley was narrow enough to choke on darkness.

Rainwater trembled in the gutters, catching the jaundiced glow of a distant streetlamp. Somewhere beyond the brick walls, the city muttered—traffic, laughter, a siren fading into the night—but here there was only the soft scrape of shoes against wet pavement.

The vampire had not meant to follow him this far.

At least, that was the lie she told herself as the man stumbled backward until his shoulders struck the wall. His breath clouded between them in quick, frightened bursts. He raised a hand as if it could keep her away.

“Please,” he whispered.

The word barely reached her.

Hunger filled everything. It had hollowed her out hours ago, turning every heartbeat in the street into a drumbeat beneath her skin. His pulse was louder than his voice—warm, frantic, alive. She could hear the blood moving through his throat.

She caught his wrist before he could run. Her fingers closed around it with terrible ease.

He cried out, twisting against her grip. The sound sharpened the hunger. For one suspended second, she stared at the vulnerable line of his neck, at the rapid flutter beneath his skin.

Then she leaned in.

Her fangs pierced him just below the jaw.

The puncture wounds were small, almost delicate at first—two dark points opening against pale flesh. His body jerked hard, hands clutching at her coat, but the struggle weakened as she drank. Heat flooded her mouth: salt, iron, life. It rushed into her with the force of a storm, easing the cold ache in her veins and replacing it with something fierce and bright.

The man’s resistance faltered.

His fingers slipped from her shoulders. His breaths became thin, uneven threads. The frantic hammering of his heart slowed beneath the roar of her hunger.

She should have stopped.

She knew that.

But the scent of blood clung to the air, rich and intoxicating, and every swallow made restraint feel more distant. His knees buckled. She held him upright without thinking, one arm wrapped around his back as though she were supporting a drunken friend rather than draining the strength from his body.

At last, a faint sound escaped him—less a plea than a breath.

That broke through.

She tore herself away.

He sagged against the wall, his head lolling to one side. Two puncture wounds marked his neck, blood welling slowly before the rain began to dilute it into thin red trails. His face had gone gray beneath the alley’s shadows. Each breath came shallowly, his chest rising with visible effort.

The vampire stood over him, trembling.

The hunger was quieter now, but not gone. It never truly left.

She pressed a hand over the wounds, feeling his weak pulse flutter beneath her palm. Still alive. Barely.

From the mouth of the alley came the distant sound of footsteps.

She vanished into the dark before anyone could see the stain on her lips—or the man she had left behind, trembling in the rain.

Mara knew it was close when the air changed.

Not colder—colder would have been merciful. This was a pressure, a dense, breathless weight that settled over her shoulders and pushed her deeper into the mud. The forest around her stood perfectly still. No insects. No wind in the leaves. Even her own ragged breathing sounded too loud.

She ran anyway.

Branches whipped her face, but she barely felt them. Every sense had narrowed to the pounding of her boots and the certainty that something moved behind her without making a sound.

Then pain opened across her back.

She screamed and stumbled forward. There had been no impact, no shape in the dark, no warning except the sudden sensation of skin parting beneath invisible claws. Heat spilled down between her shoulder blades, soaking her shirt. The wound burned for one terrible second, then turned cold, as if fingers of ice had been pressed into it.

Mara spun, clutching a tree trunk for balance.

“Who’s there?”

The words disappeared into the black trunks.

Nothing answered. Nothing stood in the path. Moonlight lay pale over roots and wet leaves, untouched.

But the air in front of her trembled.

A second blow struck her ribs. She felt it before she heard it: a crushing inward force, sharp enough to steal the breath from her lungs. Her body folded around the pain. Something scraped along her side, leaving a line of fire that became wet warmth beneath her palm.

She backed away, staring into emptiness.

That was the worst part. If she could see it, she could measure it. Give it teeth, eyes, a height. She could pretend it obeyed the rules of things with bodies.

Instead, the darkness was full of possibilities.

Every shadow might have been its arm. Every gap between trees might have been its mouth. She could hear no footsteps, no snarl, no breath—but she began to feel its presence as a prickling across her skin, the way prey must feel a predator’s gaze before it turns its head.

Her ankle caught on a root. She fell hard, palms slapping into the mud.

Behind her, leaves bent.

Not rustled. Bent.

One by one, they pressed flat as though something enormous and weightless were passing over them.

Mara crawled, sobbing now, dragging one leg behind her. A raw pressure grazed her calf. She jerked away just as three parallel cuts appeared through her trousers, blood darkening the fabric. The pain arrived late, deep and electric, racing from her leg into her spine.

She did not look back again.

She understood, suddenly, that the creature did not need to hurry. It could touch her whenever it wanted. It could stand inches from her face while she pleaded with the empty forest. It could watch every trembling breath, every desperate attempt to escape, and she would never know where to aim her fear.

That knowledge chased her harder than anything with feet.

The hall smelled of wet stone, lamp oil, and fear.

Mara stood in the center of it with iron around her wrists.

Across the chamber, beneath the black banners of the Regent, her friends knelt in a row.

Tomas stared at the floor, his bruised mouth set in the stubborn line she knew too well. He had always looked like that before a fight—quiet, annoyed, as if violence were an inconvenience interrupting his day.

Elian was shaking. Not visibly, not enough for the soldiers to notice, perhaps, but Mara saw the small tremor in his shoulders. He was trying to smile at her. Trying to make it easier.

And Sera—

Sera met Mara’s eyes and did not look away.

The Regent sat above them on a raised stone dais, one gloved hand resting against his cheek. He looked bored.

“You have been difficult,” he said.

Mara’s throat was dry. “You burned three villages to make a point.”

“And yet you still misunderstand the lesson.” He nodded toward the prisoners. “Rebellion is an expensive habit. I thought I might let you pay a portion of its cost.”

A guard stepped forward carrying a narrow wooden box.

Inside lay three ivory markers.

On each one was carved a name.

TOMAS.

ELIAN.

SERA.

Mara stared at them until the letters blurred.

“No,” she said.

The Regent’s smile barely moved. “Choose one.”

“No.”

“Then all three die.”

The words struck the room and stayed there.

Elian sucked in a breath. Tomas finally looked up. Sera’s jaw tightened.

Mara pulled against the chains. Metal bit into the skin of her wrists. “You want information? You want me to kneel? Fine. I’ll give you anything.”

“I don’t want anything from you except a choice.”

“You can’t make me do this.”

“I already have.”

The Regent gestured lazily. A soldier drew his sword.

The sound of steel leaving its sheath made Elian flinch.

Mara’s heart began to hammer so violently that she thought it might break her ribs. She tried to think, to find some hidden angle in the room: the guards at the doors, the distance to the weapons rack, the old crack in the floor beneath the dais. There had to be something. A signal. A distraction. Some trick she had missed.

But there were twelve soldiers.

Her hands were bound.

Her friends were kneeling with ropes around their throats.

And the Regent was waiting.

Tomas spoke first.

“Pick me.”

Mara shut her eyes.

“No.”

“Mara.” His voice was rough but steady. “Pick me.”

“Don’t listen to him,” Elian said quickly. “He’s always wanted to die dramatically. It’s a personality defect.”

Tomas gave a humorless breath that might have been a laugh.

Elian’s voice cracked on the next words. “Pick me instead.”

Mara opened her eyes.

He was crying now. Tears ran through the dirt on his cheeks, but he kept looking at her, desperate to be brave for her. “I’m not—I’m not as useful as they are. Tomas can fight. Sera knows the mountain routes. I’m just—”

“You’re not just anything,” Mara said.

The words came out broken.

Sera said nothing.

That was worse.

Mara turned to her. “Sera.”

Sera’s expression softened. For one terrible second, Mara saw not the hardened scout with blood on her boots and scars across her knuckles, but the girl who had shared stolen apples with her behind the old mill. The girl who had once sworn, at thirteen years old, that they would die old and furious together.

“Don’t,” Sera said quietly.

“I can’t—”

“Don’t let him turn us into weapons against you.”

The Regent sighed. “How noble. How predictable.”

He rose from his chair and descended the steps. His boots clicked slowly over the stone. When he reached Mara, he took one of the ivory markers from the box and held it between two fingers.

“You believe refusing is an act of love,” he said. “But refusal is merely another choice. If you do not select one, you select all of them.”

He placed the marker in her blood-slick palm.

It read ELIAN.

Mara threw it to the ground.

The Regent nodded.

A soldier seized Elian by the hair and dragged him upright.

“Elian!” Mara screamed.

The sword touched his throat.

“Wait,” Tomas said.

Everyone froze.

Tomas looked at Mara, and she saw terror in him at last. Not fear of death. Fear for her.

“You choose,” he said. “Because if you don’t, he gets to say he killed us all.”

Mara sobbed once, sharply, as if she had been struck.

Sera closed her eyes.

Elian whispered, “Please.”

The box stood open beside her.

Three names.

Three lives.

Three people who had trusted her with their secrets, their wounds, their futures. Tomas, who had carried her out of a burning house when she was sixteen. Elian, who had stayed awake through every nightmare after her brother died. Sera, who had crossed half the kingdom to find her when everyone else believed Mara was gone.

Her hand hovered over the markers.

She could not breathe.

Tomas.

Elian.

Sera.

The letters seemed to crawl.

“I’m sorry,” Mara whispered.

No one heard her but herself.

Then she took Sera’s marker.

For a moment, the hall was utterly silent.

Sera opened her eyes.

Mara tried to say her name, but her mouth would not work.

The Regent took the ivory piece from her fingers. “There. You see? Civilization is built on necessary sacrifices.”

Sera was brought to her feet.

Tomas began to struggle against his ropes, roaring wordlessly. Elian cried out and tried to lunge after her. Guards slammed them both to their knees.

“Mara,” Sera said.

Mara looked at her.

Sera’s face was pale. Her lips trembled once. Then she forced herself still.

“It wasn’t you,” Sera said.

But it was.

Mara knew it was.

The executioner raised his blade.

She saw every detail with unbearable clarity: the nicked edge of the sword, the leather wrapped around the man’s grip, the black hair stuck to Sera’s damp cheek. She saw Sera inhale.

Then the blade came down.

The sound was wet and final.

Blood struck the stone in a broad dark arc.

Elian screamed.

Tomas made no sound at all. He stared at the spreading red beneath Sera’s fallen body, his face emptied of everything except disbelief.

Mara dropped to her knees.

The chains rattled around her wrists as she reached toward Sera, though she was far away, impossibly far. Her hands slipped in blood when they hit the floor.

The Regent stepped around the growing pool as though avoiding rainwater.

“Take the survivors,” he said.

Only then did Tomas look at Mara.

There was no accusation in his eyes.

That was the cruelty of it.

There was only grief.

Mara bowed over her bloodied hands and began to shake so hard that the guards had to drag her from the hall.

Elian was shaking. Not visibly, not enough for the soldiers to notice, perhaps, but Mara saw the small tremor in his shoulders. He was trying to smile at her. Trying to make it easier.

And Sera—

Sera met Mara’s eyes and did not look away.

The Regent sat above them on a raised stone dais, one gloved hand resting against his cheek. He looked bored.

“You have been difficult,” he said.

Mara’s throat was dry. “You burned three villages to make a point.”

“And yet you still misunderstand the lesson.” He nodded toward the prisoners. “Rebellion is an expensive habit. I thought I might let you pay a portion of its cost.”

A guard stepped forward carrying a narrow wooden box.

Inside lay three ivory markers.

On each one was carved a name.

TOMAS.

ELIAN.

SERA.

Mara stared at them until the letters blurred.

“No,” she said.

The Regent’s smile barely moved. “Choose one.”

“No.”

“Then all three die.”

The words struck the room and stayed there.

Elian sucked in a breath. Tomas finally looked up. Sera’s jaw tightened.

Mara pulled against the chains. Metal bit into the skin of her wrists. “You want information? You want me to kneel? Fine. I’ll give you anything.”

“I don’t want anything from you except a choice.”

“You can’t make me do this.”

“I already have.”

The Regent gestured lazily. A soldier drew his sword.

The sound of steel leaving its sheath made Elian flinch.

Mara’s heart began to hammer so violently that she thought it might break her ribs. She tried to think, to find some hidden angle in the room: the guards at the doors, the distance to the weapons rack, the old crack in the floor beneath the dais. There had to be something. A signal. A distraction. Some trick she had missed.

But there were twelve soldiers.

Her hands were bound.

Her friends were kneeling with ropes around their throats.

And the Regent was waiting.

Tomas spoke first.

“Pick me.”

Mara shut her eyes.

“No.”

“Mara.” His voice was rough but steady. “Pick me.”

“Don’t listen to him,” Elian said quickly. “He’s always wanted to die dramatically. It’s a personality defect.”

Tomas gave a humorless breath that might have been a laugh.

Elian’s voice cracked on the next words. “Pick me instead.”

Mara opened her eyes.

He was crying now. Tears ran through the dirt on his cheeks, but he kept looking at her, desperate to be brave for her. “I’m not—I’m not as useful as they are. Tomas can fight. Sera knows the mountain routes. I’m just—”

“You’re not just anything,” Mara said.

The words came out broken.

Sera said nothing.

That was worse.

Mara turned to her. “Sera.”

Sera’s expression softened. For one terrible second, Mara saw not the hardened scout with blood on her boots and scars across her knuckles, but the girl who had shared stolen apples with her behind the old mill. The girl who had once sworn, at thirteen years old, that they would die old and furious together.

“Don’t,” Sera said quietly.

“I can’t—”

“Don’t let him turn us into weapons against you.”

The Regent sighed. “How noble. How predictable.”

He rose from his chair and descended the steps. His boots clicked slowly over the stone. When he reached Mara, he took one of the ivory markers from the box and held it between two fingers.

“You believe refusing is an act of love,” he said. “But refusal is merely another choice. If you do not select one, you select all of them.”

He placed the marker in her blood-slick palm.

It read ELIAN.

Mara threw it to the ground.

The Regent nodded.

A soldier seized Elian by the hair and dragged him upright.

“Elian!” Mara screamed.

The sword touched his throat.

“Wait,” Tomas said.

Everyone froze.

Tomas looked at Mara, and she saw terror in him at last. Not fear of death. Fear for her.

“You choose,” he said. “Because if you don’t, he gets to say he killed us all.”

Mara sobbed once, sharply, as if she had been struck.

Sera closed her eyes.

Elian whispered, “Please.”

The box stood open beside her.

Three names.

Three lives.

Three people who had trusted her with their secrets, their wounds, their futures. Tomas, who had carried her out of a burning house when she was sixteen. Elian, who had stayed awake through every nightmare after her brother died. Sera, who had crossed half the kingdom to find her when everyone else believed Mara was gone.

Her hand hovered over the markers.

She could not breathe.

Tomas.

Elian.

Sera.

The letters seemed to crawl.

“I’m sorry,” Mara whispered.

No one heard her but herself.

Then she took Sera’s marker.

For a moment, the hall was utterly silent.

Sera opened her eyes.

Mara tried to say her name, but her mouth would not work.

The Regent took the ivory piece from her fingers. “There. You see? Civilization is built on necessary sacrifices.”

Sera was brought to her feet.

Tomas began to struggle against his ropes, roaring wordlessly. Elian cried out and tried to lunge after her. Guards slammed them both to their knees.

“Mara,” Sera said.

Mara looked at her.

Sera’s face was pale. Her lips trembled once. Then she forced herself still.

“It wasn’t you,” Sera said.

But it was.

Mara knew it was.

The executioner raised his blade.

She saw every detail with unbearable clarity: the nicked edge of the sword, the leather wrapped around the man’s grip, the black hair stuck to Sera’s damp cheek. She saw Sera inhale.

Then the blade came down.

The sound was wet and final.

Blood struck the stone in a broad dark arc.

Elian screamed.

Tomas made no sound at all. He stared at the spreading red beneath Sera’s fallen body, his face emptied of everything except disbelief.

Mara dropped to her knees.

The chains rattled around her wrists as she reached toward Sera, though she was far away, impossibly far. Her hands slipped in blood when they hit the floor.

The Regent stepped around the growing pool as though avoiding rainwater.

“Take the survivors,” he said.

Only then did Tomas look at Mara.

There was no accusation in his eyes.

That was the cruelty of it.

There was only grief.

Mara bowed over her bloodied hands and began to shake so hard that the guards had to drag her from the hall.

Martin first noticed the smell in October.

It drifted over the fence on cold evenings, a sour-sweet odor beneath the usual smoke from burning leaves. His neighbor, Raymond Vale, always blamed it on his old furnace.

“Thing’s older than both of us,” Raymond would say with a mild laugh.

Martin had known Raymond for six years. He was quiet, punctual, and painfully polite. He trimmed his hedges with a ruler. He brought in Martin’s bins when Martin forgot. He wore neatly pressed shirts even when he was only mowing the lawn.

Nobody would have called him frightening.

That was why Martin entered the house when he saw the back door standing open.

It was late November. Wind rattled bare branches against the windows, and Raymond’s porch light flickered weakly over the yard. Martin had come over to return a package mistakenly delivered to his address.

“Ray?” he called from the kitchen.

No answer.

The house was unnaturally clean. Not tidy—sterile. The counters shone. The air smelled of bleach and something metallic hidden beneath it. A soft humming came from somewhere below his feet.

Martin set the package down and told himself to leave. Raymond was probably in the basement. Maybe the old man had forgotten the door.

Then he heard a sound beneath the hum.

A faint, irregular clink.

Like glass tapping glass.

At the end of the hallway was a basement door Martin had never seen open. It had three locks on it: a brass deadbolt, a sliding chain, and a thick padlock hanging from a metal latch. Tonight, all three were undone.

The door stood open an inch.

Cold air breathed through the crack.

Martin descended because fear does strange things to people. It can make them run. It can make them freeze.

And sometimes it convinces them that the worst thing imaginable cannot possibly be waiting at the bottom of a staircase.

The basement steps were steep and narrow. The humming grew louder. He found the switch at the bottom, but when he flipped it, nothing happened.

Then, farther ahead, a light clicked on.

A yellow bulb hung over a workbench. The basement beyond it was divided by plastic sheeting, the sort painters used to keep dust from spreading. A narrow opening had been cut into the middle.

The humming came from a small freezer against the wall.

The clinking came again.

Martin stepped through the plastic.

At first, he thought he had stumbled into Raymond’s workshop.

There were shelves, carefully labeled. Boxes. Cabinets. A long table covered with tools arranged in straight, immaculate rows. The floor had been scrubbed so thoroughly that the concrete looked pale and raw.

Then he saw the photographs.

They covered an entire wall.

Not framed pictures—prints pinned in grids, dozens upon dozens of them. Faces stared out from each image: women, men, teenagers, elderly people. Some were smiling in candid snapshots. Some were taken from a distance on sidewalks or in cafés. Others showed frightened faces caught in harsh basement light.

Most had dates written beneath them.

Some dates had been crossed out in red ink.

Martin moved closer despite himself.

Under each photograph was a small brass plaque.

A name.

An age.

A date.

He recognized one of the faces.

Elena Morris, the college student who had disappeared two years earlier after her car was found abandoned near the river. Her mother had handed out flyers at the grocery store for months.

The plaque beneath Elena’s photograph read:

**ELENA MORRIS — 21 — APRIL 14**

Beside the photo was a clear display case.

Inside lay a silver necklace with a tiny blue stone at its center.

Martin remembered the necklace from the missing-person posters.

His stomach clenched.

He turned slowly.

The shelves were not filled with tools.

They were filled with trophies.

Rows of watches, each one stopped at a different time. Wallets stacked by color. Rings threaded on hooks. A child’s pink hair clip in a glass jar. A row of driver’s licenses mounted beneath clear plastic, their faces staring upward like the dead preserved beneath ice.

On another shelf stood labeled jars. Martin did not look closely at first. He thought they contained buttons, maybe coins.

Then he saw the pale curve floating in yellowed liquid.

A tooth.

The jar beside it held several more.

Another contained a lock of hair, braided with a faded red ribbon.

The clinking came from a mobile hanging in the corner.

It turned slowly in the draft from the furnace. Dozens of small objects dangled from wire: rings, keys, charms, pieces of jewelry. Among them were tiny white fragments that tapped gently against each other.

Martin realized they were knuckles.

He stumbled backward, knocking into the workbench.

A framed newspaper clipping fell from the wall and shattered on the floor. Its headline stared up at him.

**THIRD HIKER MISSING IN COUNTY PARK**

Beneath it, someone had written in black marker:

**THEY NEVER LOOK UNDER THEIR FEET.**

The freezer hummed beside him.

Its lid was secured with a heavy chain. Condensation slicked the metal. A dark stain had dried around the base and seeped into a crack in the concrete.

Martin did not open it.

He did not need to.

Behind the freezer, partly hidden by the plastic sheeting, was a narrow door painted the same color as the basement wall. From the other side came a soft scraping sound.

Once.

Twice.

Then a muffled voice.

“Hello?”

Martin stopped breathing.

The voice came again, weak and hoarse.

“Please. Is someone there?”

Every instinct in him screamed to run, but he crossed the room and reached for the knob.

A hand closed around his wrist.

Raymond Vale stood behind him.

Martin had not heard him come down the stairs.

Raymond’s shirt sleeves were rolled neatly to the elbows. There was a thin streak of red-brown beneath one fingernail. His expression was not angry.

That was the worst part.

He looked disappointed.

“I wish you hadn’t come down here,” Raymond said.

Martin stared at the hand gripping him. It was calm, steady, almost gentle.

From behind the hidden door, someone began to sob.

Raymond sighed.

“You seem like a good man, Martin. You always brought your bins in before the rain.”

Martin ripped his arm free and ran.

He crashed through the plastic sheets, slipped on the stairs, caught himself against the wall, and scrambled upward. Behind him, Raymond did not shout. He did not chase immediately.

He only called, in the same mild voice he used across the fence:

“Martin. You’ve forgotten your package.”

Martin burst through the open back door and into the night, screaming for help until porch lights flickered on up and down the street.

By the time the police arrived, Raymond Vale’s house was still lit from basement to attic.

The back door remained open.

And from the dark below, beneath the steady hum of the freezer, came the faint sound of glass tapping glass.

The first alarm had barely finished its second shriek before the cellblock became a storm.

Red emergency lights pulsed across concrete walls, turning every face into a flickering mask. Doors stood half-open where locks had failed or been forced, and inmates poured into the corridor in a rush of orange uniforms, improvised weapons clutched in their hands—sharpened scraps of metal, broken broom handles, lengths of chain torn from maintenance cages.

A guard went down near the control booth, hit from the side by a rolling knot of bodies. His riot shield clattered away across the floor. Another officer dragged him by the vest toward a security door as inmates hammered against the advancing line of guards. Batons cracked against arms and shoulders. Shields slammed forward, driving men back for a moment, only for the crowd to surge again with a roar that drowned out the alarms.

The air was thick with pepper spray and smoke from a burning mattress somewhere deeper in the wing. It stung the eyes, blurred the lights, and made everyone cough. Prisoners shouted names, threats, and orders over one another. Guards barked commands that vanished beneath the noise.

Near the stairwell, two inmates had cornered an officer against the railings. He swung his baton wildly, catching one across the jaw, but the second rushed him low and drove him into the metal bars. Other guards forced their way through, shields raised, striking hard enough to clear space around him. The crowd scattered, regrouped, then threw itself back into the fight.

Above it all, behind reinforced glass, the control room lights flashed as officers struggled to restore lockdown. Cameras swung uselessly over smoke-filled corridors. Every few seconds, another metallic crash echoed through the block—something breaking, something giving way.

The prison, built to contain violence, seemed to have turned inside out. Its walls still stood, its razor wire still gleamed beyond the narrow windows, but inside, order had collapsed into a savage, echoing battle of bodies, noise, and fear.

Rain threaded down the hotel window in silver lines, turning the city below into a blur of smeared neon and brake lights.

On the room’s little round table, Mara had arranged her tools with the care of someone setting cutlery for dinner. Cloths. Oil. A compact pistol broken neatly into pieces. Across from her, Ivo sat on the edge of the bed, polishing a slim blade with a hand towel that had once been white.

The television murmured with the sound off. Some game show host grinned soundlessly at the room.

“You know what I miss?” Ivo said.

Mara didn’t look up. “Indoor plumbing?”

“Professionalism.”

She gave a small laugh. “You’re cleaning a knife with a hotel towel.”

“It’s absorbent.”

“It has ‘Property of the Monarch’ stitched into it.”

“Then the Monarch should have bought better towels.”

Mara slid a cloth through the barrel of her pistol, inspecting it against the lamp. “Professionalism,” she repeated. “That’s what you miss.”

“People used to have style.” Ivo held the blade up, examining his reflection in it. “A little imagination. Now everybody wants noise. Explosions. Messages carved into walls. Very theatrical.”

“You say that like you’ve never worn a mask.”

“I wore one mask. Once.”

“It was a bird.”

“It was a very good bird.”

Mara’s mouth twitched.

Ivo leaned back on one hand. “So. What’s your favorite?”

“My favorite what?”

“Way to do the work.”

She fitted the pistol back together with quiet clicks. “That’s an ugly question.”

“We have ugly jobs.”

“We have jobs. You’re the one who insists on making them a personality.”

He considered this. “Fair.”

For a moment there was only rain, the air conditioner rattling, and the soft mechanical sound of Mara checking the slide.

Then she said, “Clean.”

Ivo waited.

“Clean is my favorite.” She set the pistol aside and reached for a fresh cloth. “No spectacle. No panic. No one trying to be remembered. You arrive, you leave, and afterward people argue about whether you were ever there.”

Ivo nodded slowly. “Very you.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means you’d rather be a rumor than a person.”

Mara looked at him then. Her expression was mild, but it made him smile.

“And you,” she said. “You like an audience.”

“I like certainty.”

“You like drama.”

“Certainty can be dramatic.”

“No, Ivo. You can be dramatic.”

He shrugged, unbothered. “Fine. I like close work.”

“Of course you do.”

“There’s honesty in it.”

“There’s something wrong with you.”

“There’s something wrong with both of us. Mine is just better dressed.”

Mara shook her head and began wiping down the magazine. “Close work is messy.”

“Not if you know what you’re doing.”

“That’s exactly the kind of thing people say before they ruin a perfectly good suit.”

Ivo looked down at his charcoal jacket hanging over the desk chair. “This suit has survived worse.”

“Your suit has survived because you send your laundry bills to shell companies.”

“Planning ahead is not a crime.”

“Depends who’s asking.”

The game show audience on the television erupted into silent applause. Colored lights flashed across the host’s broad smile.

Ivo watched it for a while. “You ever think about quitting?”

“No.”

“Not even once?”

Mara paused.

Outside, a siren wailed somewhere far below, then faded into the rain.

The graveyard had been full by midnight.

By the third bell, it was empty.

Not empty in the way of peace, with bones sleeping under earth and names fading from weathered stones. Empty in the way a battlefield is empty after the carrion birds have lifted—every mound split, every coffin overturned, every dark hollow breathing out the wet smell of opened flesh.

Mordain stood at the center of it all, barefoot in the mud.

Rain hissed against the black iron bowl before him, turning the blood inside to steam. The symbols he had carved into the ground glimmered faintly beneath the water: not runes, not any script meant for human mouths. They curled and uncurled like pale worms beneath the surface of the earth.

He raised one hand.

The wind stopped.

For a moment, nothing moved but the rain.

Then a finger thrust up through the soil.

It was gray and swollen, its nail blackened and half-gone. Another hand followed, clawing at the mud with frantic, boneless effort. The dead man beneath the nearest grave pulled himself free by degrees: first the hands, then arms slick with gravewater, then a face ruined by burial.

His jaw hung from a thread of skin. Beetles crawled from his empty eye socket. When he opened his mouth, soil spilled out in a long, wet stream.

Mordain did not look at him.

“Stand,” he said.

The corpse obeyed.

All around the graveyard, the earth began to convulse.

Mounds split open with sounds like coughing lungs. Rotten bodies rolled from their coffins in funeral silks reduced to brown rags. Some were little more than yellowed skeletons with strips of flesh dangling from their ribs. Others had been buried recently enough to retain the swollen likeness of humanity: cheeks collapsed inward, lips peeled back from dark gums, hair hanging in damp ropes around their faces.

They rose anyway.

A woman in a child’s burial dress dragged herself from a shallow grave, one leg ending at the knee in a splintered stump. A soldier climbed from the earth with an arrow still lodged beneath his collarbone. An old priest came up last, his white robes black with rot, his fingers clutching a broken holy symbol as though he had tried to hold it against whatever waited in the dark below.

Their eyes opened.

There was no fire in them.

No blue witchlight, no red ember glow. That would have been kinder. Their eyes were simply empty, yet fixed upon Mordain with the awful attention of things that could no longer think but had not been allowed to forget.

The necromancer lowered his hand, and something answered beneath the graves.

It was not a voice. Voices belonged to throats, breath, and living intent. This came from deeper down, from the wet black places between roots and coffins, from the long silence where the dead had waited for their names to be forgotten.

The corpses shuddered.

Several began to weep.

Not tears—there was not enough moisture left in them for that—but thick, dark fluid seeped from their ruined eyes. Their mouths opened in unison, and the sound that emerged was a low, broken moan, full of soil and old pain.

Mordain smiled.

Beyond the cemetery wall, torches burned along the road to the city. Men with spears were gathering there. Priests. Soldiers. Farmers clutching rusted sickles. They would come at dawn, brave in their numbers and prayers.

By dawn, there would be no graves left in the valley.

The dead turned toward the road.

Their joints cracked as they moved. Flesh slid from bone. The smell of them rolled through the rain—sweet, rancid, and thick enough to taste.

And beneath their dragging feet, the earth whispered its hunger.

The warehouse smelled of oil, wet concrete, and old smoke. Six figures stood in a loose circle beneath a flickering light, their faces half-hidden beneath hoods and shadows. At the center was Malik, the youngest of them, his hands shaking despite the fists he kept clenched at his sides.

The leader, Rook, stepped close enough that Malik could smell liquor on his breath.

“You want the colors?” Rook asked quietly. “You want us to call you family?”

Malik nodded.

Rook pointed toward a man on his knees near the far wall—someone from a rival block, bound and bleeding from the mouth. The man’s eyes were wide, darting from face to face, searching for mercy that none of them intended to give.

“Then prove it,” Rook said.

The others closed in around Malik, not touching him, but trapping him all the same. Their silence was heavier than shouting. One of them muttered that anyone could talk tough on the corner; anyone could wear a jacket. Loyalty meant doing something that could not be taken back.

Malik hesitated. Rook’s expression hardened.

“Walk away,” the leader said, “and you walk away alone. But if you stay, there’s no turning on us. Ever.”

The weapon was shoved into Malik’s hand. It felt too heavy, cold against his palm. The captive begged, his voice cracking, but the gang members laughed without humor. Rook leaned close to Malik’s ear.

“Do it,” he whispered. “Or we’ll know you’re weak.”

For a long second, Malik stood frozen between fear and the desperate need to belong. Then, under the weight of their stares and threats, he acted.

The violence was quick, ugly, and irreversible. When it was over, the warehouse fell silent except for Malik’s ragged breathing. Blood darkened the floor beneath him. Rook gripped his shoulder with approval, while the others nodded as though something sacred had been completed.

But Malik did not feel accepted. He felt hollow.

The gang had not given him a family. They had made sure he had nowhere else to go.

I had chosen the blue plates because they made everything look harmless.

The roast lay in its dark sauce beside a fan of glazed carrots, the potatoes whipped smooth and shining with butter. Candlelight trembled in the crystal glasses. Beyond the windows, rain pressed itself against the garden like a crowd listening at a door.

Edwin cut another piece of meat.

“You’ve outdone yourself,” he said.

His praise was always a little too careful, as though he expected applause in return. He lifted the fork, chewed, swallowed. Across the table, his wedding ring caught the candlelight whenever he moved his hand.

I smiled. “You say that every time.”

“Because it’s true every time.”

The poison had no taste worth noticing. That was the mercy of it—or the cruelty. I had spent months imagining this moment, and in every version he had looked up at once, understanding blooming in his face like a stain. In reality, he reached for the salt.

He began telling me about the solicitor.

“The papers are nearly sorted,” he said. “Once the sale goes through, I’ll be free of the place by autumn.”

Free. The word sat between us.

Outside, thunder rolled somewhere beyond the fields. Edwin spoke over it, talking about the city apartment he intended to buy, the clubs he would rejoin, the new life he would begin without the burden of an old house and an older marriage.

I watched him take another bite.

At first, there was nothing. His color remained good. His voice still carried that smooth, assured rhythm he used when he believed himself in command. He dabbed the corner of his mouth with his napkin.

Then he paused.

It was no more than a hesitation between sentences.

“You all right?” I asked.

He looked at me with faint irritation. “Of course.”

But his hand had stopped midway toward his glass.

A blush had risen in his cheeks—not warmth, not embarrassment, but an uneven red that spread beneath the skin. He flexed his fingers as if they had stiffened around the stem of the wineglass. His eyes narrowed.

“Perhaps it’s the wine,” he said.

“You barely touched it.”

He tried to laugh, but the sound came out thin. He set the glass down too quickly, and red wine sloshed onto the white cloth. For a moment, we both watched it spread.

Edwin pressed two fingers against his throat.

“There’s a strange feeling,” he said.

“What sort of feeling?”

He opened his mouth, then seemed to reconsider. Pride was one of the last things to leave him. “Heat.”

The candles had burned lower. Their flames leaned in the draft, bending toward him.

His breathing changed before he seemed to notice it: shallower, deliberate. He sat straighter in his chair, as if posture alone could correct whatever had gone wrong inside him. A bead of sweat appeared at his temple, ran slowly down beside his ear.

“You look pale,” I said.

“I’m not pale.”

“No,” I said softly. “You’re not.”

His complexion had shifted from flushed to gray beneath the red. He pushed his plate away. The fork scraped sharply across the porcelain.

He stared at his hands.

They trembled now. Not violently—just enough that the spoon beside his plate ticked against the edge each time his knuckles brushed the tablecloth.

“What did you put in this?” he asked.

There it was.

Not understanding, exactly. Not yet. Only suspicion, wounded and incredulous. He looked from the food to me, his eyes brightening with a frightened kind of focus.

“I made dinner,” I said.

His chair legs shrieked against the floor as he stood. He made it halfway up before his knees gave way. He caught himself on the table, scattering the silverware. One candle toppled, its flame extinguishing in a pool of spilled wine.

“Call someone,” he said.

His voice had changed. The polished authority was gone; the words came rough and broken around his breathing.

I remained seated.

“Please,” he said.

The rain whispered at the windows. Somewhere in the house, the old clock began to strike nine.

Edwin sank back into his chair, though he seemed not to choose it. His chest rose and fell in quick, uneven pulls. His eyes moved around the dining room—the portraits, the sideboard, the curtains I had selected twenty years ago—as if the familiar objects might provide testimony on his behalf.

“You can’t,” he murmured.

I thought of all the times he had said those same words to me. You can’t leave. You can’t manage. You can’t prove anything.

His lips had begun to lose their color.

“I can,” I said.

He looked at me then, truly looked at me, perhaps for the first time in years.

The storm flashed white across the windows. In that instant, his face seemed terribly old.

He reached across the table, fingers searching over the linen. I watched them stop a few inches from my hand.

Then the darkness returned, and the candles continued to burn.

Outside, thunder rolled somewhere beyond the fields. Edwin spoke over it, talking about the city apartment he intended to buy, the clubs he would rejoin, the new life he would begin without the burden of an old house and an older marriage.

I watched him take another bite.

At first, there was nothing. His color remained good. His voice still carried that smooth, assured rhythm he used when he believed himself in command. He dabbed the corner of his mouth with his napkin.

Then he paused.

It was no more than a hesitation between sentences.

“You all right?” I asked.

He looked at me with faint irritation. “Of course.”

But his hand had stopped midway toward his glass.

A blush had risen in his cheeks—not warmth, not embarrassment, but an uneven red that spread beneath the skin. He flexed his fingers as if they had stiffened around the stem of the wineglass. His eyes narrowed.

“Perhaps it’s the wine,” he said.

“You barely touched it.”

He tried to laugh, but the sound came out thin. He set the glass down too quickly, and red wine sloshed onto the white cloth. For a moment, we both watched it spread.

Edwin pressed two fingers against his throat.

“There’s a strange feeling,” he said.

“What sort of feeling?”

He opened his mouth, then seemed to reconsider. Pride was one of the last things to leave him. “Heat.”

The candles had burned lower. Their flames leaned in the draft, bending toward him.

His breathing changed before he seemed to notice it: shallower, deliberate. He sat straighter in his chair, as if posture alone could correct whatever had gone wrong inside him. A bead of sweat appeared at his temple, ran slowly down beside his ear.

“You look pale,” I said.

“I’m not pale.”

“No,” I said softly. “You’re not.”

His complexion had shifted from flushed to gray beneath the red. He pushed his plate away. The fork scraped sharply across the porcelain.

He stared at his hands.

They trembled now. Not violently—just enough that the spoon beside his plate ticked against the edge each time his knuckles brushed the tablecloth.

“What did you put in this?” he asked.

There it was.

Not understanding, exactly. Not yet. Only suspicion, wounded and incredulous. He looked from the food to me, his eyes brightening with a frightened kind of focus.

“I made dinner,” I said.

His chair legs shrieked against the floor as he stood. He made it halfway up before his knees gave way. He caught himself on the table, scattering the silverware. One candle toppled, its flame extinguishing in a pool of spilled wine.

“Call someone,” he said.

His voice had changed. The polished authority was gone; the words came rough and broken around his breathing.

I remained seated.

“Please,” he said.

The rain whispered at the windows. Somewhere in the house, the old clock began to strike nine.

Edwin sank back into his chair, though he seemed not to choose it. His chest rose and fell in quick, uneven pulls. His eyes moved around the dining room—the portraits, the sideboard, the curtains I had selected twenty years ago—as if the familiar objects might provide testimony on his behalf.

“You can’t,” he murmured.

I thought of all the times he had said those same words to me. You can’t leave. You can’t manage. You can’t prove anything.

His lips had begun to lose their color.

“I can,” I said.

He looked at me then, truly looked at me, perhaps for the first time in years.

The storm flashed white across the windows. In that instant, his face seemed terribly old.

He reached across the table, fingers searching over the linen. I watched them stop a few inches from my hand.

Then the darkness returned, and the candles continued to burn.

The dawn was gray and windless, the sea flat as hammered lead.

A plank jutted from the starboard rail of the *Black Mercy*, its end hanging over water that churned with dark, circling shapes. Fins broke the surface one by one, slicing lazy arcs through the foam. The crew stood in a silent ring around the condemned man.

Elias Vane had been first mate three days ago.

Now his wrists were bound behind his back, his shirt torn, his face swollen purple from the captain’s fist. He stared at the plank as though it were a gallows beam.

“Captain,” he whispered. His voice shook so badly that the word barely formed. “Captain, I only asked the men for their share. I never meant—”

Captain Rook leaned against the rail, immaculate in his weather-dark coat. A pistol rested loosely in one hand.

“You meant to take my ship,” Rook said. “You meant to put a blade in my back while I slept.”

“No.” Elias swallowed. Below him, something large struck the hull with a dull, wet thump. The sharks had caught the scent of blood from the butchered fish tossed overboard at first light. “Please. Maroon me. Put me ashore. I’ll never raise a hand against you again.”

Rook’s expression did not change.

“Walk.”

The boatswain cut the rope around Elias’s ankles.

For a moment, Elias did not move. His bare feet gripped the deck boards. Then two sailors stepped behind him, their faces turned away, and shoved him toward the plank.

He stumbled onto it.

The wood creaked beneath his weight. The sea seemed impossibly far below, though it was only a dozen feet. Sharks circled directly beneath him now—gray backs, pale bellies, black eyes rolling just beneath the surface.

Elias took one step.

Then another.

Each was slower than the last.

By the time his toes reached the splintered end, his whole body was trembling. Tears shone on his cheeks. He looked back at the crew—men who had drunk with him, fought beside him, called him brother.

“Someone,” he begged. “For God’s sake, someone—”

Nobody moved.

Captain Rook lifted his pistol.

Elias flinched at the click of the hammer.

Then he fell.

His scream tore across the silent water and ended in a splash.

For one heartbeat, the sea closed over him.

Then it erupted.

A shark struck from below, throwing a froth of red into the air. Elias surfaced shrieking, clawing at the water with bound hands, his face white with terror. Something seized his leg and dragged him sideways. He vanished again beneath thrashing tails and churning foam.

The water boiled.

Blood spread in dark ribbons around the ship. The crew heard muffled cries, then a wet, terrible crunch beneath the surface. A severed hand broke free of the frenzy and drifted briefly in the wake before being pulled under.

Within moments, the sharks had scattered, leaving only crimson water and a few scraps of cloth bobbing on the waves.

Captain Rook looked over the rail for a long time.

Then he turned to his crew.

“Let it be remembered,” he said quietly, “that the *Black Mercy* has but one captain.”

No one answered.

The sea did that for them, lapping softly against the hull.

At first, Elias only heard the knocking.

Three slow taps from beneath the floorboards.

He told himself it was the pipes. The house was old; the beams shifted in the cold, and the wind worried at the shutters like fingernails. He repeated these explanations every night as he sat rigid in his chair, staring at the black mouth of the fireplace.

Tap.

Tap.

Tap.

But there were no pipes beneath the parlor.

Only the cellar.

Only the place where he had buried Mara after he could not bear the sound of her screaming anymore.

He had not meant to kill her. That was what he whispered each time the knocking began. He had meant to frighten her, to silence her, to make her understand that she could not leave him and take everything with her. The knife had been in his hand before he remembered lifting it. The blood had been on his sleeves before he remembered the warmth of it.

Now, every night, the house remembered for him.

The first time he saw her, she was standing at the end of the hallway.

Elias woke near dawn, his cheek stuck to the desk by dried sweat, the lamps burned down to blue-black stubs. The corridor beyond his study was dark except for a pale shape near the staircase.

“Mara?” he said.

The shape tilted its head.

Her hair hung in wet ropes around her face. Her dress was the same yellow one she had worn that night, though it was soaked through at the chest, dark and glistening. A red stain spread slowly over the fabric, blooming again and again as if the wound had never stopped opening.

Elias could not move.

She lifted one hand. Her fingers were black beneath the nails, packed with cellar dirt.

Then she pointed at him.

The lamps went out.

He screamed until morning.

After that, she appeared everywhere.

In the mirror, standing behind him with her throat slit open in a smile.

In the windows, pale-faced beyond the glass though rain poured outside and there were no footprints in the mud.

In his soup, where the surface trembled and reflected her staring eye instead of his own face.

He stopped sleeping. He nailed blankets over the mirrors. He stuffed wax into his ears, but still, beneath the silence, he heard her voice.

Not words at first.

Just breathing.

A wet, delicate breath from beneath the floor.

Then, one evening, as he crouched over the kitchen sink scrubbing his hands raw, she spoke.

“You left me in the dark.”

Elias froze.

The water running over his fingers turned red.

He stared at it, gasping. Blood poured from the faucet, thick and hot, carrying little clumps of black soil into the basin. The smell rose around him: iron, rot, damp earth.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered.

The voice came from inside the drain.

“You listened.”

He stumbled backward, striking the table. On it lay the knife.

He had thrown that knife into the river.

It was clean now. Polished. Waiting.

Elias began to laugh then, a thin, broken sound that startled him more than anything else. He laughed until tears ran down his face, until he could barely breathe. He picked up the knife and held it to his chest, as though he could keep it from turning against him.

“I didn’t listen,” he said. “I couldn’t.”

The cellar door creaked open.

Cold air rolled through the kitchen, carrying the scent of grave soil and something sweetly rotten. Elias stared into the blackness beyond the doorway.

A faint light flickered below.

Not candlelight.

Moonlight, perhaps—though there were no windows in the cellar.

He descended one step at a time.

The walls seemed narrower than before. The shadows clung to his shoulders. At the bottom, he found the earth floor disturbed, the boards he had laid over the shallow grave splintered and pushed aside.

Mara sat in the hole.

Her head rested against the dirt wall. Her eyes were open, milky and accusing. Worms moved slowly through her hair.

“You said you loved me,” she murmured.

Elias fell to his knees.

“I did.”

Her jaw cracked as she smiled.

“Then why did you bury me alone?”

He reached for her, sobbing, desperate to take her hand, to explain, to undo the single terrible moment that had devoured every moment after it.

His fingers closed around air.

The cellar was empty.

There was no grave. No broken boards. No body.

Only a large mirror leaning against the far wall.

In it, Elias saw himself kneeling in the dirt, clutching the knife.

And behind him, close enough that her breath stirred the hair at his neck, Mara stood smiling.

This time, when he screamed, the whole house answered.

The body lay in the alley like the city had finally coughed up something it couldn’t digest.

Rainwater crawled around the dead man’s shoes, black with oil and old cigarette ash. It pooled in the cracks of the pavement, carrying little scraps of paper toward the storm drain like messages nobody wanted to read. Above him, the fire escapes clung to the brick walls like rusted ribs.

He’d been opened up bad. Not messy in the amateur sense—this was careful work, the kind done by somebody who understood where all the important parts were kept. His shirt had gone dark and stiff. His face had the gray, waxy look of an abandoned tenement: hollow windows, no lights behind them, plumbing shot to hell.

I’d seen men die prettier. Usually they took a piece of the city with them: a scream, a siren, a crowd gathering behind yellow tape. This one had gone quiet. The alley swallowed him whole, same as it swallowed loose change, broken promises, and every drunk who mistook a doorway for a bed.

The victim’s hand was curled around nothing.

That was the part that bothered me.

The dead usually held on to something—a photograph, a name, a last lie. This guy had empty fingers, clenched tight as a landlord’s fist. Whatever he’d had, whoever he’d trusted, had been taken before the blood cooled.

A neon sign across the street blinked red through the rain.

VACANCY.

That was the city’s joke. There was always room for one more corpse.

The sirens stopped at midnight.

That was how Mara knew the hunt had entered its final hour.

She stumbled through the remains of an elevated train station, boots splashing in black rainwater pooled between cracked tiles. Above her, the city glowed in layers: advertisements crawling across the towers, spotlights combing the smog, the gold-white spire of the Directorate rising over everything like a blade.

RUN, citizen, sang a cheerful voice from hidden speakers. Your freedom is worth watching.

Mara pressed one hand against her side. Blood seeped warm between her fingers, though she couldn’t remember when the hunter’s first shot had found her. The tracking band locked around her wrist flashed red.

Nineteen minutes.

She had survived nine hours.

That was longer than most.

Ahead, the station ended in a collapsed platform overlooking the river. There had once been a bridge there, but only half its skeleton remained, twisted out over the water. Mara climbed anyway, hauling herself over damp steel beams as drones buzzed somewhere beyond the fog.

“Runner Mara Venn,” came a man’s voice, amplified but close. “You are impressive.”

She froze.

The rain ticked against the metal.

Below, the river churned around the drowned foundations of old buildings. Fifty stories down. Too far to jump.

Mara turned slowly.

He stood at the far end of the platform beneath a broken departure board.

Hunter Vale wore the traditional white coat, immaculate despite the rain. His mask was polished silver, featureless except for a narrow black visor. A rifle rested lazily in one gloved hand. Behind him, two camera drones hovered, their red lenses fixed on Mara.

The city was watching.

Every screen in every apartment, every bar, every factory break room would be carrying this moment live. Citizens would be placing final bets. Some would be cheering for her. Most would be cheering for him.

“You have a contract,” Mara said. Her voice came out ragged.

“I do.”

“One capture. Alive.”

Vale tilted his head, as if admiring the detail. “Alive enough to identify.”

Mara looked toward the broken bridge.

Then she ran.

Vale fired.

The shot struck the beam beside her foot, showering sparks. She leapt the gap anyway, landing hard on the narrow skeleton of the bridge. Metal groaned beneath her weight. She scrambled forward, hands slipping on rain-slick steel.

A second shot took the rail beside her.

A third struck her shoulder.

Pain spun her sideways. She caught herself on one arm, dangling above the river, legs kicking at empty air. Her wounded shoulder screamed as she clung to the beam.

Behind her, Vale’s boots rang against the metal.

“No more running,” he said.

Mara tried to pull herself up. Her fingers slid. For one breathless second, she thought she might make it.

Then Vale stepped on her hand.

Not hard enough to crush it. Just enough.

Her grip broke.

She fell only a few feet before a cable snapped taut around her waist. The impact stole her breath. She hung over the river, swinging beneath the bridge framework as the crowd noise burst from the drones’ speakers—millions of voices compressed into a roar.

Vale crouched above her and reeled in the capture line.

Mara clawed at the cable as he drew her upward, inch by humiliating inch, until she lay shivering on the steel at his feet.

The hunter placed one boot between her shoulder blades.

“Runner Mara Venn,” he announced to the drones, “captured at zero hours, fifty-three minutes.”

The cameras moved closer.

A bright gold seal flashed across their lenses: DIRECTORATE HUNT — VERIFIED.

The sirens stopped at midnight.

That was how Mara knew the hunt had entered its final hour.

She stumbled through the remains of an elevated train station, boots splashing in black rainwater pooled between cracked tiles. RUN, citizen, sang a cheerful voice from hidden speakers. Your freedom is worth watching.

Mara pressed one hand against her side. Blood seeped warm between her fingers, though she couldn’t remember when the hunter’s first shot had found her. The tracking band locked around her wrist flashed red.

Nineteen minutes.

She had survived nine hours.

That was longer than most.

Ahead, the station ended in a collapsed platform overlooking the river. There had once been a bridge there, but only half its skeleton remained, twisted out over the water. Mara climbed anyway, hauling herself over damp steel beams as drones buzzed somewhere beyond the fog.

“Runner Mara Venn,” came a man’s voice, amplified but close. “You are impressive.”

She froze.

The rain ticked against the metal.

Mara turned slowly.

He stood at the far end of the platform beneath a broken departure board.

The city was watching.

Every screen in every apartment, every bar, every factory break room would be carrying this moment live. Citizens would be placing final bets. Some would be cheering for her. Most would be cheering for him.

“I do.”

“One capture. Alive.”

Vale tilted his head, as if admiring the detail. “Alive enough to identify.”
